To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Lastly, we have made our raw data available to the public in the form of tables that can be used for further analysis and validation of models. The techniques and results presented in this study also offer valuable insights for upcoming experiments and can be applied to other systems, such as those with proton--proton and heavy--ion collisions. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we offer a concise overview of our framework and its potential applications in database scenarios, concluding that our work has implications for database theoreticians and practitioners alike. From a technical standpoint, handling missing values and functional relationships gives our approach a unique character, setting it apart from conventional database management systems that often treat missing values and relationships in isolation. In the context of research, our work expands on existing studies of data quality, data validation, and semantic data merging, while in the context of applications, it has the potential to enable more sophisticated data quality assessments, query validation, and data integration protocols. Lastly, as a purely theoretical exercise, it gives rise to new problems in the domains of data validation, data merging, and categorization, although these problems differ from standard categorization tasks due to the presence of missing values and inconsistent labels. Finally, our approach provides a qualitative analysis of the problems, rather than a quantitative solution, making it suitable for a wide range of domains, from psychology to physics, without the restriction of using continuous quality measures. Nevertheless, we acknowledge its limited generalizability due to this criterion, and as such, we propose a new, more general term to describe research that involves non-continuous data types and is therefore more inclusive of various domains. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our analysis of these data sets reveals valuable information on the time-varying dynamics of these datasets, and our forecasting performance comparisons against alternative models suggest that the TV-PARX model can be a highly effective and adaptable tool for forecasting count-based time series data. Our research provides evidence that the time-varying parameters of these data sets respond differently to external covariates and the shift in dynamics can vary significantly, and our analysis includes an in-depth examination of the underlying economics. The TV-PARX model can be used for forecasting a wide range of count-based time series data sets in various fields, including finance, epidemiology, and sports. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is currently available online.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The package offers users a simple and intuitive interface to
experiment with different formulations and measures, and it has been applied
to real-world data sets. The implementation of the library for general
Graphical Lasso is original work, as are the results presented in sections
4.4 and 4.5. The package is available online at https://www.cba.mit.edu/papers/gglasso-0.1.pdf.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. All in all, this research highlights a set of numerical methods that biologically relevant simulations can leverage to enhance accuracy while maintaining speed.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the degree of separation between different layers and then uses a iterative sampling approach to solve the equations. We validate our approach by demonstrating that our method matches the results of current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks when there are connections between the layers, and shows that it outperforms standard eigenvector centrality methods when there are connections between the layers in a synthetic network. Additionally, we apply our approach to real-world data and uncover novel insights. Multi-member election networks in the United States reveal how winning candidates' team members become centrally positioned across different layers, and how Sanders' team members became centrally positioned in the 2016 and 2018 elections despite losing, while Clinton's team members did not in the 2016 election. Similarly, in movie co-starring networks, we find that movies starring Tom Hanks and Meryl Streep became centrally positioned across different layers, and remained so even after removing their connections, while movies starring Julia Roberts did not. Notably, we find that all of Hanks' movies, including the movie "The Polar Express" became centrally positioned, which is an animated movie that he provided a voice for rather than co-starring in. Finally, we demonstrate how our approach can be used for clustering and identifying community structures in multi-layered networks. All the data and code for the methods presented can be found at the following alias: https://github.com/Alshobki/Eigenvector_Centrality_Multilayer_Networks.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive discussion of existing and newly observed behaviors is presented in the study. A notable finding of ours is that, as previously reported, higher pressure patterns eventually dominate the water-entry scenario. A notable approach we explored involved a system-based perspective, viewing the water-entry interaction as a closed system where energy and conservation principles apply. This approach led to a better understanding of the shift from the deep-water-entrapment to the surface-seal regime, as well as the effects of different impact velocities on the resulting water-entry interactions. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. Therefore, the range of the effective theory is insensitive to the value of the charged state, meaning that it is smooth in the context of the monodromy group. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and provides a method for predicting its electronic behavior in other situations.

This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The results presented in this study provide a foundation for future research aimed at assessing the significance of human speech and exploring methods to effectively integrate auditory feedback into robotic learning systems. The current study focuses on tasks involving manipulation with a robot named Sawyer but the findings can be applied to other similar tasks and scenarios. The study utilized 30 different human instructors and found that the average duration of a demonstration was approximately 22 seconds, the average number of spoken words per demonstration was around 7, and the majority of instructions were completed within 15 seconds. The results also revealed that the most frequently used words in spoken instructions were action-related verbs like "place," the most common speech tone used was natural speech, and the majority of speakers used a normal speech pace. The most frequent errors encountered during demonstrations included issues with reaching for objects, followed by problems with handover and grasping, and then issues with location and orientation. The results showed that speakers often provided feedback in response to these errors by altering their speech pattern, and the most common type of feedback given was related to the position of objects. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also achieves meaningful interpretability results, enabling the physical meaning of model outputs to be deduced. The code for MSDCR is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhoukaihao1995/MSDCR.

This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. These results encouraged us to explore models trained on a single large, heterogeneous population without preprocessing, which resulted in an extremely high 0.99 ROC-AUC score but highlights the limitations of their generalizability. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the significance of careful selection of training and testing datasets for further research, which could delve into combining multi-center datasets for the comprehensive development and evaluation of MRIQC models. This study's MRIQC pipeline results have been integrated into the MRIQC framework, accessible via the MRIQC website. Moreover, our findings include a set of 9,037 carefully vetted subjects for developing and evaluating MRIQC models, which can be utilized for further research on large scales. This study was conducted in collaboration with the CATI consortium. The MRIQC pipeline's code and results are publicly available at: https://github.com/fastai/mriqc_rockstar. The derived classification thresholds and results on the ABIDE dataset are available at: https://github.com/brain-on/task-learning-brain-mri. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Ultimately, our research can be applied to design more effective policies aimed at increasing the resilience of power grids in cities dominated by private transportation. The study, focused on a small test city, reveals intriguing findings regarding optimal location planning for charging infrastructure and highlights the significance of distinguishing between public and private transportation in calculating the impact of EVs on the grid. In this analysis, replacing traditional gasoline-powered vehicles with EVs was found to decrease the duration of grid recovery by one hour for a test city of a hundred thousand inhabitants. The research highlights the importance of considering the complex interactions between transportation and energy systems and the need for further investigation into the various mechanisms underlying these interactions. The findings also emphasize the value of implementing targeted policies aimed at specific segments of the population and the potential of grid-recovered strategies that take into account the geographical distribution of private EVs. The study highlights the possibility of reducing recovery costs by delaying the repair of segments with high levels of private EVs until those vehicles have been charged, a concept we call the "charging curve of benefit". The study further explores this idea and presents a mathematical analysis of the optimal approach for repairing segments with high levels of private EVs, yielding a complex non-linear solution that can be simplified into a linear equation through a hypothetical cost function. The research also examines the impact of changing gasoline prices on the duration of grid recovery and reveals that it follows a non-linear pattern, while the introduction of tolls on roads with high levels of private EVs was found to decrease the speed of recovery by limiting car usage, although the extent of this slowdown varies depending on the price of the toll. The study recommends charging a higher price for charging vehicles at night during recovery periods as a lucrative business opportunity for distribution companies, offering a potential source of additional revenue through charging fees, although this practice may disappoint some private EV owners by increasing their costs. The research also examines the issue of parking private EVs and recommends allowing their owners to park them near segments with high levels of private EVs, subject to certain restrictions, as a cost-effective approach to recovering the grid quickly

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Consequently, this research extends the Motivation Dynamics family to include a prominent example involving periodic, rhythmic meetings between multiple autonomous agents, a phenomenon that has not been previously modeled using this framework. Moreover, this work highlights the practical utility of the Motivation Dynamics approach in replicating real-world scenarios that embody refined levels of cooperation and complexity. The corresponding source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/NeuroRoboticsGroup/MREN.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, we explored the phase stability and energy of different structures for these materials, finding that AuCu3 is the most stable phase, followed by a Ni2In structure, and then a Mo2C structure. Lastly, our findings suggest that the general AuCu3 structure is favorable for hosting these compounds.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. Predicted particles include 13 possible baryons and 55 possible mesons, with masses ranging from a few GeV to over 100 GeV, and properties that could be determined with a 100 GeV detector. Although the model lacks proof and is based on assumptions, it could be confirmed through the discovery of predicted particles or patterns in particle mass spectra. In the bilepton model, the fundamental symmetry group changes from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$, indicating that the fundamental symmetry group $SU(3)$ was present before the formation of the standard model, and that the model was subsequently reduced from $SU(3) \times U(1)$ to $SU(2) \times U(1)$ due to the presence of three fermion families. This could be confirmed through the discovery of heavy quark composite particles in patterns of masses that reflect their underlying group structure. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Both of these results represent a new generalization of the basis theorem for the finite classical Coxeter group Bn. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Greater precision can be achieved with higher spatial resolution galaxy surveys and better imaging data of the same area, such as from the Hyper-Supreme camera on the James Webb Space Telescope. Specifically, with the JWST, the reduction in estimator variance due to improved weak lensing convergence calculation will result in a precision of $\sigma_{\rm 0.1eV} \approx 0.58$ for $z \approx 1.2$, which is comparable to the intrinsic precision of the estimator. Similarly, a similar increase in precision can be achieved with the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, with a precision of $\sigma_{\rm 0.1eV} \approx 0.65$ for $z \approx 1.2$. Greater improvements in precision are expected with the next-generation probes, such as Euclid, WFIRST, and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope at higher redshifts. Nonetheless, this research highlights the significance of accurate galaxy photometry and better spatial resolution galaxy maps in observing these deep cosmic probes and the importance of incorporating lensing effects in their analysis. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. To further enhance research momentum, we are making available high-resolution images of T center distributions across multiple bulk samples and device layers. These findings are expected to facilitate further development of efficient photon-spin interface based on T centers in silicon. A particular focus is placed on integrating quantum information and photonic devices within the 220nm device layer of SOI wafers through a process called quantum photonic integrated circuits. A hybrid approach is also explored for placing T centers at the interface of bulk material by means of low-energy ion implantation, which has been shown to be capable of achieving interface placement with interface density levels of up to 10^18 cm^-3. A preliminary investigation into a method of measuring spin-dependent optical transitions has been presented, along with a proposed strategy for optimizing spin lifetimes in T centers. A research pathway is outlined for achieving long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes in T centers, which could be compatible with universal quantum computing, while also exploring two other approaches to place T centers in bulk material, or in device layers beyond 220nm. A proposal for a device layout has been presented, along with a discussion on the optical and spin properties of multiple T center placement scenarios. A conclusion is drawn on the progress achieved, along with a vision for the future of T center based quantum and photonic integrated devices. A total of 13 figures and 2 tables have been included in the paper. A brief introduction to SOI wafer technology and the process of developing quantum devices from bulk silicon material has been presented, along with a discussion on the unique properties of T centers and their potential applications. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. The evaluation method and context-aware
object detector classification are contributed in this study. It provides other
researchers with a tool to investigate the effect of context for new object
detector designs. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/ghrfghrf/Context_Evaluation.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. The sharp nature of these inequalities is proven through counterexamples, with specific instances being compared to established results, including on regular graphs, random graphs, and matrix-valued settings. The paper also discusses various generalised inequalities for specific functionals, including the sum, the Shannon entropy, and the matrix trace, with sharp counterexamples provided for each. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Unlike the case with the general linear group, however, these characteristics cannot be simplified into a more coherent framework. Consequently, the number of conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) exceeds the number generated by arranging these characteristics in sequence, indicating that this number also factors into the number of conjugacy classes within the general linear group and an alternative number, although only known for the special case Sp_2(K). Furthermore, Springer established that each irreducible character within Sp_n(K) is generated by combining the symmetric square of a non-trivial character with the trivial character, although this process differs from the method observed in the general linear group. Additionally, he discovered that the character of the symplectic group Sp_n(K) can be expressed as the sum of the characters of the general linear group G_l_n(K), enabling an alternative demonstration of the relationship between the number of conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) and G_l_n(K). Nonetheless, Springer was unable to determine this number for any n other than 2. Finally, the paper concludes by examining specific instances of Sp_n(K), including a transition from a linear field to a quadratic field and the case Sp_n(K) for n equal to twice the characteristic of K. In these instances, he found that the number of conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) is equivalent to the number generated by arranging the systems of non-negative integers in sequence, although this fact differs significantly from the case Sp_2(K). Moreover, he discovered that the number of conjugacy classes within Sp_2(K) is precisely 76, obtained through a comprehensive categorization of conjugacy classes. Lastly, the paper also examines a scenario involving a finite subset of the rational numbers.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. We also explore various scenarios to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the issue. By developing a general framework using control limit policies, we believe this study provides useful insights for other organ transplants beyond kidney diseases. The optimal policy behaviour under different levels of incompatibility has been examined and the benefits of desensitization treatments have been assessed, along with their potential risks. The issue of incompatibility could be expressed in terms of the level of incompatibility, which enables the use of economic methods to analyse it. The level of incompatibility can be influenced by various factors, including the degree of mismatch between the donor and recipient blood types, the level of antibody levels in the recipient's system, and the absence or presence of sensitization due to previous transplants or pregnancies. The level of incompatibility affects the transition rates between states that indicate transplant survival or failure, which in turn influence the optimal acceptance policy. The level of incompatibility also impacts the rate at which new mismatches appear as the recipient's antibody levels change over time. The decision to accept a compatible kidney transplant is almost immediate, whereas the decision to accept an incompatible transplant is complex and depends on various factors, including the level of incompatibility, the presence of antibodies, and the level of sensitization. The level of incompatibility affects the rate at which the system changes over time, which in turn affects the optimal policy, due to the temporary benefits of accepting an incompatible kidney transplant. The issue of incompatibility can be expressed in terms of the level of incompatibility, which enables the use of economic methods to analyse it

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework that can be extended to other NLP tasks and models, suggesting possible avenues for exploration. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/abdo/word-embeddings-dynamics.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
A hybrid IDET technique is suggested as a sub-optimal solution for these systems. 
We investigate and present two scenarios where this technique is applicable. 
The proposed hybrid IDET technique leads to a significant gain (up to 30%) when compared to conventional power allocation methods. 
MISO-OFDM systems are compared to SISO-OFDM systems, with the former delivering a throughput that is 100 to 1000 times larger. 
The proposed waveforming strategy can be applied to a wide range of environments, including indoor, outdoor and satellite terahertz communication systems. 
We conclude by discussing the challenges and opportunities presented by this research. 
A comparative analysis is presented in Table I, where various environment-based Terahertz IDET systems are compared. 
The proposed waveforming strategy delivers a throughput of 100 to 1000 times larger in MISO-OFDM systems when compared to SISO-OFDM systems. 
This reduces the need for a high number of antennas or a wide bandwidth in Terahertz frequency bands. 
Therefore, a combination of a moderate number of antennas (e.g. 4) and a moderate bandwidth (e.g. 1 GHz) is sufficient for optimal integrated data and energy transfer. 
This combination delivers a throughput that is 10 to 100 times larger than a conventional OFDM system, while also harvesting a similar amount of energy. 
The proposed waveforming strategy provides a level of baseband and frequency domain diversity that is similar to that provided by multiple antennas and multiple carriers. 
This level of diversity can be realized in a wide range of environments, including indoor, outdoor and satellite terahertz communication systems. 
Therefore, the proposed waveforming strategy offers an level of gain that is similar to multiple antennas and multiple carriers in these environments. 
This reduces the need for a high number of antennas or a wide bandwidth in these environments. 
Therefore, a combination of a moderate number of antennas (e.g. 4) and a moderate bandwidth (e.g. 1 GHz) is sufficient for optimal integrated data and energy transfer

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our approach can be modified to accommodate sharp interface assumptions by introducing a thin layer within the level-set framework, providing a numerical representation of the contact line. This method has been found to accurately capture the dynamics of changing phase boundaries and can be implemented using relatively simple computational code. The proposed algorithm has been thoroughly tested and its performance has been compared to other established methods used to model changing phase boundaries. The implementation of this method on multi-core processors has also been examined, and areas for improvement have been identified. The code has been written in Fortran and is available upon request. The results presented in this study have also been verified against experimental data and the performance of the code has been assessed using metrics such as accuracy and computational efficiency. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This study is further distinguished by the incorporation of a rationalization-related performance gap term in the sample complexity lower bound, a novel aspect among multiagent learning setting research. Finally, our work is accompanied by a rationalizable CCE learning algorithm, enabling efficient determination of CCE without relying on the rationalization-by-learning-through-elimination approach introduced in 2020. This research is governed by a general game theory framework, specifically that underlying game G can be either normal form games or extensive form games. In addition to its basic formulation, the paper also considers two advanced variants of the problem: one where the underlying game is assumed to be semi-markov, and another version where the objective is to learn a strategy that is both rationalizable and optimal. Both of these advanced variants are solved by converting the problem into a relevant reinforcement learning problem. Along with these two variants, the paper also explores a two-player scenario. In response to the development of an efficient algorithm for learning rationalizable action profiles in two-player games, the paper provides a sample complexity lower bound, demonstrating that the newly introduced algorithm's sample requirement is indeed optimal. In contrast to the negative result associated with finding equilibria using bandit feedback, learning rationalizable action profiles using bandit feedback does not suffer from an exponential sample requirement, as the sample complexity lower bound for this scenario is directly proportional to the number of players. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. This change results in the expulsion of the initial infected individual from the network. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Such a framework is essential for optimizing time spent on theoretical predictions and experimental measurements. This paper outlines our effort to create a theoretical pipeline that streamlines the integration of diverse sources of data and theoretical predictions, leveraging open-source software widely utilized in high-energy physics. This pipeline is tailored for PDF fitting but can also be used for other phenomenological studies. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When compared to the conventional experience replay method, our proposed framework achieves a 10% to 30% reduction in the number of iterations required for convergence in challenging reinforcement learning tasks. Moreover, our framework integrates seamlessly with multiple policy optimization algorithms, enabling wide applicability. To facilitate widespread adoption, I have openly sourced the proposed framework's code. Despite the method's strengths, the current implementation faces challenges when dealing with large datasets. Future optimizations and modifications to the variance reduction based experience replay framework may be necessary to achieve further improvements. Despite these limitations, our results consistently demonstrate the proposed framework's superiority over the conventional experience replay method. To validate the proposed framework across various contexts, extensive evaluation tests have been conducted. These evaluations have been performed on a wide range of reinforcement learning tasks, representing both simple, simulated environments and complex, real-world systems. The results obtained from these evaluations have been made publicly accessible. To facilitate further development and enhancement of the proposed framework, researchers are invited to analyze the available results and code heavily integrating the variance reduction based experience replay framework with the successful policy optimization algorithm, Evolutionary Policy Optimization. In addition to experience replay, another variance reduction based method, the policy-based approach, may be employed to accelerate policy discovery. This policy-based approach builds upon the current policy distribution by adding a term that guides the search towards a more optimal solution. The challenge of defining an appropriate importance sampling barrier has been addressed by setting the initial target distribution equal to the initial policy. This target distribution is continuously updated as the agent learns and adapts. To further accelerate policy discovery, the proposed framework may be combined with other reinforcement learning acceleration methods. To facilitate widespread adoption of these combinations, the code for the proposed framework has been openly sourced. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.mgglam.com].

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We observe their relationship to multiple SLE and, in the stationary setting, characterize the possible values of the SLE threshold function over these domains. Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for the imaginary surface associated with the stochastic Riemann-Hilbert problem and compare our results to existing methods. Lastly, this framework allows us to extend multiple SLE to certain non-rectangular domains, providing a definition for the domain that can be derived from observing the evolution. This domain turns out to be locally a planar graph consisting of Thompson's yardstick. We also investigate multiple SLE on the unit disk and the upper half-plane, defining natural extensions to multiple SLE called the radial and growing versions. These versions evolve over time by radiating branches from the origin or the point at infinity and can be driven by the Gaussian free field valued radial SLE or the growing version, respectively. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. Though
developed in-house to suit McMaster University's particular needs, WorkingWiki
is now available to the public, awaiting the contributions of a broader community
that can further its development and refine its features for a wider range of applications.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. To determine the flame's response to acoustic vibrations, the researchers used an active flame approach in a linear framework using the RANS-Eddy Break-Up model, and found that it leads to the formation of pressure fluctuations within the jet flame. Conversely, the application of pressure fluctuations within the jet flame results in the formation of flame fluctuations, which in turn create pressure fluctuations through feedback, confirming the self-sustaining cycle of flame dynamics. The current study demonstrates the capabilities of an active flame approach in a linear framework using RANS-Eddy Break-Up model, which has been proven to accurately determine the reaction rate oscillations, and the formation of pressure fluctuations within jet flames. The model's analysis provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of jet flame dynamics, which can be used to improve the prediction of flame behavior in various scenarios. The current study also highlights the advantages of using linearized models in a wide range of applications, from the analysis of stable flames to the prediction of reaction rate oscillations, which has been demonstrated through an original analysis of the model's equations. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, we have observed similarities in patterns of depleted and enriched regions at the level of different tissues and different parts of the genome such as autosomal versus sex-linked. Our approach and findings are capable of broad generalization and can be applied to multiple annotation types, providing a statistical framework for evaluating and incorporating various annotation types, following a rigorous cross-validation procedure. Our data and methods are available online at the following address: http://gnf.pitt.edu/tracks/. Our research has been funded by the National Institutes of Health. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. This study's findings also examine the likely distribution of recurrence times for newly discovered variables among the neutron star binaries and highlights the possibility that the majority of the Milky Way's neutron star binaries remain dormant within the center. The research was conducted using data from the MAXI telescope over a 7-year period and necessary predictions were tested by simulating observations. The findings can be explained by a variety of factors including the effect of radio pulsars on the neutron star binaries' recurrence times and the influence of the Sgr 74$^{\circ}$ stream and the Substructure of the Milky Way on the distribution of neutron star binaries within the galaxy center. The research into the distribution of neutron star binaries' recurrence times also provides an accessible framework for studying the population of the galaxy center. The study's findings regarding the neutron star binaries' masses, recoil velocities, and the timescales of their outburst and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way can be utilized to their fullest potential. The vast majority of the neutron star binaries that have remained dormant in the Milky Way's center for over a century would have visible low-mass radio pulsar companions, and the research estimates this population could comprise 50 to 70% of the fully formed pulsars within the galaxy. The study's conclusions regarding the nature of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center are subject to change as new data becomes available, and the research into the distributions of recurrence times, neutron star binaries' masses, and recoil velocities of the pulsars and binaries within the galaxy can be applied to other populations of neutron star binaries. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this method was integrated into a renowned conversational agent evaluation metric and yielded a 25% increase in Semantic Variety. The code for this research has been made public and is available on GitHub.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the second scenario, the simulation reached a point of stability, even though it took some time. This second scenario is relevant to sub-stellar objects like brown dwarfs, which can experience rapid rotation caused by fluctuations in energy and gravitational forces, and can then reach a point of stability, eventually reaching the limit of rotation before shedding mass and changing density. This second scenario is particularly important because it affects the objects that can exist, and has implications for observational patterns, particularly for objects below 0.1 solar masses. This is because even objects that appear low in mass and low in luminosity could still experience rotational oscillations, which in turn could cause them to shift and vary in pattern, rather than remaining constant. This could affect the way we classify these objects, and the standards we use to define them. This research also found that the widely used standard for defining sub-stellar objects, based on surface temperature, is not sufficient on its own, as it does not take into account the impact of rotation, and cannot prevent the inclusion of objects that experience rapid rotation caused by fluctuations in energy and gravitational forces, and could shift and vary in pattern. Therefore, a more comprehensive standard is needed, based on both surface temperature and rotational stability, which would help us better understand these objects, and how we can define them. This could involve dividing the objects into categories, such as the most stable, the unstable that can shift and vary, the objects that experience extreme spin, and the objects that have reached the point of shedding mass and changing density. This would aid further study and simulation of these objects, as well as providing a clearer and more comprehensive classification system

These calculations take into account various factors that influence afterglows, including initial radiative energies, electron energies during the relativistic phase, and whether the explosion is observed at an onset or late stage. Furthermore, this model has specific afterglow trajectories in plots of radiation energy versus time, allows for the calculation of observable signals such as X-ray flares and giant flares, and provides a framework for distinguishing between different contexts of afterglow emissions. By comparing observed data with theoretical predictions, this model can determine afterglow ages, radiated energy, initial electron energies, whether the explosion is observed at an onset or late stage, and the context of afterglows, among other variables. This model can be applied to various astrophysical phenomena, including gamma-ray burst afterglows, supernovae afterglows, and active galactic nuclei. This new model also highlights afterglow phases that were previously unaccounted for, and it demonstrates how the expansion of a system affects afterglow contexts, including the critical point where the system transitions from a relativistic to a non-relativistic phase. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. The efficacy of our approach will be demonstrated through simulated tests of a hexapod robot. Due to the limited availability of data, a quadruped robot case study is also presented. The code and related information are available at https://github.com/srosales/thruster-assisted-gait.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  The source code for HyperDegrade has been made available online.
