Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. To make the approach more effective, future developments could focus on incorporating temporal information and better handling of intense point sources. Despite its limitations, this study demonstrates a groundbreaking way to analyze Fermi data and provides code available for public use. Additionally, the team created a sharpened all-sky map from a year's worth of observations, which can be found on the Fermi Science Portal.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We further present a practical application to route planning in geographic regions. We conclude by analyzing the potential and limitations of action sequences in addressing various optimization challenges and propose potential future research directions. In addition, we provide detailed algorithms for some of the mentioned scenarios including graph matching, Boolean satisfiability, and route planning, and evaluate their performance in simulated environments. We also discuss connections to existing research and techniques, and propose novel interpretations of well-known optimization problems as action sequences rather than static problems. In doing so, we introduce a new framework based on action sequences that can be applied to a broad range of domains, offering a novel perspective on the challenge of honesty and providing a way to certify the validity of solutions obtained. In the process, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework on several well-known optimization problems and suggest future research on a wide range of other domains including multicut in graph theory, clustering, and scheduling. In the appendix, we provide a detailed characterization of first-best action sequences under uncertainty, and examine the connection between action sequences and individual quasi-linearity, offering a new perspective on the challenge of honesty and providing a way to certify the validity of solutions obtained. We also examine the challenge of honesty from a theoretical perspective, providing a precise bound on achievable honesty for combinatorial optimization domains and proposing a payment scheme based on action sequences that is individually rational

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings, accompanied by a newly developed D&D dataset containing conversations, intentions, and a fictional world, contribute to the advancement of both chatbots and models of a learning mind. They provide a critically needed framework for evaluating chatbots through the prism of a role-playing game, offering an alternative to intent-based conversations that incorporate a rich, dynamic educational environment. Moreover, our work offers a response to the challenge of generating complex, abstract stories, as well as a pioneering effort in transferring knowledge from simulated environments to real-world settings. Our code, dataset, and guidance on D&D are available at: https://g4cchallenge.github.io/.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. The statistical approach also reveals that the folding pathways of trefoil knots are influenced by their knot polynomial properties, which could be linked to their folding challenges. The development of this research provides a platform for investigating other types of knots and knotted proteins found in nature. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, if the developed Riemannian metric associated with $\omega$ satisfies certain geometric criteria on $T^4$, this result can be simplified to an exact proof of the infinity of its mapping class group. A second part of the note establishes that there are no smoothly distinct, irreducible, and symplectically trivial mapping classes on the blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$, given that it fulfills another, more stringent irrationality criterion which can also be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$. A related conjecture is then presented, claiming that the mapping class group of the blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is generated by the mapping class group of $T^4$ and the positive integer multiples of a specific element. A procedure for constructing many different versions of this conjecture concretely is demonstrated. Lastly, among these versions, there are some that are logically equivalent to a particular, particularly rigorous form of the initial irrationality criterion mentioned above, thereby implicitly implying that these versions are likely true, given that this form of the criterion has been consistently unsubstantiated thus far. A third part of the note is devoted to analyzing a specific class of developed Riemannian metrics associated with $\omega$ on $T^4$, consisting of the results of applying a particular transformation to the standard Riemannian metric of $T^4$. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, counterfactual data of this kind at a large scale also enables seamless extension to new perturbation types, thereby facilitating various applications such as but not limited to data augmentation across different modeling tasks, determining counterfactual boundaries, and counterfactual explanation formation. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process could lead to the creation of complex oxide heterostructures with unique properties, facilitating the reuse of expensive substrate materials and reducing fabrication costs. The specific case of GdPtSb highlights the versatility of this approach, as it results in coexistence of different epitaxial relationships between individual grains, yet remote epitaxy itself was confirmed through theoretical modeling. Finally, this study demonstrated that precise investigation of experimental conditions is necessary to understand the underlying growth mechanisms, yet experimental proof of remote epitaxy remains strong even without it. The practical application of this research is further illustrated by demonstrating the removal of the sapphire substrate to obtain a freestanding graphene/Heusler film, offering considerable scope for reducing fabrication costs and exploring new materials. The theoretical modeling also facilitates the prediction of suitable combinations of Heusler compounds and graphene substrates, enabling the design of novel materials with tailored properties. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique can be applied in real-world applications including but not limited to text-to-image generation.  The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/lingyu-gh/Single2Multi.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The framework serves as a foundational module for developing complex healthcare models, a feature validated by activity recognition expansion examples presented in the paper. The source code for FedHealth is available at https://github.com/ghru/FedHealth. This framework has significant implications for the healthcare industry, an sector characterized by vast individual differences. Consequently, FedHealth has the potential to be successfully adapted in various other healthcare scenarios. To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints. The LHC at 13-14 TeV can lead to multiple leptoquark scenarios, particularly with certain charge combinations and heavy leptoquarks, with limits set on their mass ranges. In particular, the most restrictive constraints on the mass of quark-dual leptoquarks are $m_{(3,0)} > 1424$ GeV and $m_{(3,2)} > 458$ GeV, which can be compared to prior findings by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, our research finds that the most commonly studied symmetric production process in the LHC is generally more sensitive to certain leptoquark groups than previously recognized, indicating that existing sensitivity analyses may require revision. Lastly, to facilitate further research, our constraints and insights are available through the LeptoQuark Calculator online tool. The discovery potential for asymmetric production processes at the LHC also make it suitable for pair creating with 100 TeV protons, the Future Circular Collider, which can lead to multiple leptoquark scenarios with combinations of charges (0,0), (3,2), (2,3), (3,3) with the most restrictive constraints on the mass of quark-dual leptoquarks being $m_{(3,0)} = m_{(0,3)} \approx 1424$ GeV, $m_{(3,2)} = m_{(2,3)} \approx 458$ GeV, $m_{(2,2)} \approx 671$ GeV. The optimal asymmetric production process at the 100 TeV Future Circular Collider can lead to the direct observation of heavy leptoquarks with combinations of charges (3,0), (0,3), (2,2), (2,2) requiring the existence of new physics beyond the Standard Model. We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs. Given that external factors influence line ratios, we advocate for simultaneous observations of multiple spectral lines across various astrophysical contexts. Given its complexity, we recommend maintaining 3-level system models when analyzing CI lines and consider 2-level system models to be insufficient. Given the widespread presence of CO and CI in galaxies, we propose these molecules may be ubiquitous components of intergalactic medium. Given the massive amounts of gas associated with low line ratio galaxies, we propose them as candidates with which to study intergalactic molecule physics. Given that line ratios vary with position and wavelength, we propose high dynamic range observations with sufficient spectral resolution is necessary to fully understand galaxy physics. Given the difficulty of modeling line ratios based on various external and astrophysical factors, we propose a 3-level system model as a standard for both observational and theoretical studies of CI lines. Given the general applicability of 3-level system models to various astrophysical contexts, we propose them as a tool for testing and validating such models. Given the line ratios' independence of radiative transfer models, we propose them as markers for studying dust, gas, and wind properties. Given the line ratios' response to external changes, we propose them as indicators for searching for galactic winds, active nuclei, and massive reservoirs. Given the line ratios' response to thermal balance, we propose them as markers for searching for hot dust, associated molecular and atomic gases. Given the line ratios' response to density changes, we propose them as indicators for searching for low density winds and/or gas reservoirs

Moreover, we show that the asymptotic velocity process of a system with initial data represented by discrete steps is equivalent to the ASEP speed process. Additionally, our findings include the consequence that the asymptotic velocity process of a system with initial data represented by discrete steps is exchangeable, a property that, to date, has been observed only in systems with initial data represented by parabolas. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our proposed system, built using a comprehensive set of 465 primer pairs, can store a vast amount of data in relation to its sequence cost, with an analyzed example showing the storage of a 500 MB file in approximately 87 billion bases of DNA. Our research was conducted using a state-of-the-art DNA sequencer and the results have been thoroughly compared with an alternative storage solution using a hard drive and a fingerprint-based storage system using card indices. Our proposed system outperformed these solutions in terms of sequence cost, storage capacity, and data efficiency, demonstrating the significant advantages and vast potential of DNA storage in various applications. The associated source code has been made publicly available on GitHub. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a preliminary step towards developing a learning-based model that can adapt to changing riverbed profiles, and further optimization is needed to enhance its performance. Nevertheless, our results indicate that such an approach is feasible and may be applied to other geographical areas with similar sedimentological characteristics. Lastly, as a noteworthy finding, we discover that even without considering the effects of turbulence, the PCADNN model achieves comparable prediction accuracy to the traditional method, suggesting that it effectively captures the residual variability unaccounted for by the solution of the shallow water equations. This knowledge may be utilized to improve the resolution of other machine learning models applied to similar geographical areas. Finally, our work highlights the potential of a related learning model, which could be used to develop a non-parametric riverbed profile estimator from flow velocity measurements, and we propose this model as a potential future research direction. Lastly, we conclude by outlining three potential future research avenues arising from this work. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. We also integrate our method into a process monitoring system, enabling processes to be represented as DCR graphs from which future states can be predicted, even in the presence of unknown actions. By analyzing recorded processes at different points in time, we gather insights into process evolution, revealing that processes generally evolve in predictable ways, although exceptional cases exist. These predictable patterns take various forms, and by categorizing them, we demonstrate that processes often change by modifying conditions, updating actions, or adding connections between existing processes. These typical process evolution patterns can be utilized to enhance process discovery tools, providing more accurate and adaptable process models. Although processes evolve due to exceptional events, these events are often worth analyzing as they may reveal hidden process flaws, offering opportunities for process improvement. In the process improvement phase, we propose a method to correct processes by removing process flaws, based on process change patterns and quality measures, providing multiple possible corrected process models from which the best one can be selected. We also explore the relationship between process change and process data loss, presenting a theorem that ensures process continuity even after data loss, as long as a process change threshold is respected, providing a basis for developing more efficient process discovery algorithms that prioritize process preservation over data retention. Our approach and associated results contribute to process knowledge retention, providing efficient and accurate declarative process discovery and validation methods, effective in detecting process changes and data loss, and capable of recommending suitable process change policies to ensure process preservation and continuity. These findings and techniques can be applied to various process domains and contexts, offering process knowledge retention benefits that extend beyond declarative processes to other dynamic system categories. Our process discovery and validation tools, along with test data and example answers, are available online. We also present a Java-based implementation of our approach, providing user guidance and instructions in the README file. Our process change analysis and validation methods can be used by itself, without the process discovery component, as described in the README file. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This is supported by evidence from NUV$-r$ color and S\'ersic index $n$, and provides a much-needed explanation for the downturned slope observed in the mass-star formation rate relation. Furthermore, this finding emphasizes the critical distinction between bulge-dominated star formation and disk-dominated star formation, and highlights the significance of considering the density of star formation within bulges and the mass-star formation rate relation in the context of galaxy evolution. The growth of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies also offers a possible mechanism for quenching star formation in these systems. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. A different proof of a previously known result is thus obtained. Additionally, this finding leads to the discovery that the simplicial set N_G(W) constitutes a simplicial group via the action of W on the nerve of the full subgroup functor. Furthermore, this simplicial group is naturally isomorphic to the simplicial set obtained by applying the simplicial functor N_G to the classical universal bundle W. The simplicial group N_G(W) can be viewed as a generalization of the concept of a group of loops, and it represents the identity functor on the category of simplicial groups in a universal manner. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/zwang96/SABRA.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Although primarily observational in nature, this study also included theoretical analysis of the proposed scenarios, including a discussion of possible oscillatory modes induced by tidal inertial waves and the effects of planet ingestion on the star's structure and chemical composition. Ultimately, KIC 9267654 emerges as an outlier in the context of its internal rotation, and further research is necessary to fully understand this complex phenomenon. As such, this study adds a new variable to the established set of rotation parameters for this star and provides specific recommendations for future missions and observations, including a proposed characterization of the possible substellar companion using direct imaging and a spectroscopic analysis of the star's surface layers and possible planetary remnants. Lastly, this research is relevant to ongoing and future investigations focused on a range of topics, from the distribution of angular momentum within rotating giants to the effects of planet ingestion on the chemical and structural evolution of low and intermediate mass stars. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Finally, a general framework for constructing GCM quadruples in any number of dimensions is presented. Perhaps most notably, this work's framework for GCM quadruples in one dimension generalizes the exclusive prime factorization requirement to include composite factors, with the condition that the GCM in any dimension must be a perfect square. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Notably, our approach and results are supported by graphical illustrations, numerical experiments, and a real-world example involving a nonlinear non-linear hidden Markov model. Our research finds its place within the community of machine learning at large, with potential connections to related areas like statistical learning theory and artificial general intelligence. Our code has been made publicly available at GitHub.com/ghrasoul/Learning-Dynamics-and-Structure-of-Complex-Systems-Using-GNN.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Additionally, the upgraded GP 2 compiler, coupled with a recently developed GP 2 interpreter, demonstrates the potential for program verification tools like the GP 2 validator to complete tasks significantly faster. As an appendix, a method is provided for calculating the BigArray's optimal maximum size, further enhancing the compiler's performance. Despite the compiler upgrade focusing on the GP 2 compiler, its developments are relevant and applicable to the powerset compiler. In conclusion, the GP 2 compiler upgrade has been successfully demonstrated, accompanied by open-source code available for public use.

The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. In particular, this paper demonstrates that the proposed method can lead to a model with a smaller number of categories, eliminating the need for a separate dimension reduction step, and providing a more precise estimate with better predictive performance. The proposed method's advantages make it suitable for applications involving a large number of variables, such as genetics and network analysis. The paper includes a numerical example where the Group Lasso fails to sparsity the model due to its large size, but the new method delivers a accurate and interpretable model. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. One potential application of this method is correcting faulty knowledge graph triples. To this end, we develop a simple model capable of determining whether individual knowledge graph triples are accurate, utilizing a simple metric that calculates the average model's confidence in the triple's correctness. Our findings suggest that while generally reliable, there are instances where the model misjudges correct triples as faulty. To address this, we propose a selective correction approach that only corrects triples deemed likely faulty by the model. By applying this strategy to Wikidata, we discover a significant number of previously unknown invalid triples. One interesting aspect of this finding is the verification of a previous claim made by a different researcher, who stated that their earlier analysis which had identified 10664 incorrect triples was an overestimation. Our discovery confirms this assessment, revealing the actual figure to be substantially lower. One potential issue with the approach is the presence of redundant knowledge graph triples. To address this, we develop a simple method to remove such triples, thereby improving performance in tasks that favor specificity over generality. One interesting variation of the approach involves training the model on inverse knowledge graph triples. To validate this technique, we create a simple evaluation benchmark consisting of reverse triples. One potential application of this technique is enhancing transparency in large language models by identifying the structured information behind their generated text. To achieve this, we develop a simple method to reconstruct the original knowledge graph triples from the trained models. One interesting aspect of this technique is the discovery that many of the previously uncovered invalid Wikidata triples actually represent missing inverse relationships. One potential issue with the approach is the presence of triples that contain ambiguous references. To address this, we develop a method to remove such triples, thereby improving performance in tasks that favor clarity over ambiguity.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code for the DPCRN model is available online at github.com/lingyu-93/DPCRN.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our study also examines conditions under JC-interaction-induced multipartite entanglement generation. Lastly, we discuss the potential of this scheme for scaling to larger multipartite systems. Our findings are relevant to quantum simulations involving multiple JC-systems, such as III-V semiconductor nanophotonic systems, optical interferometry, and superconducting qubits. Our research is also related to previous studies on multipartite entanglement creation via JC-interaction, notably a proposal involving multiple JC-arrays, which could potentially lead to genuinely multipartite entanglement generation via parametric amplification, although this has not been achieved in practice as of this knowledge cutoff date.

By focusing on these marked patterns, one can map the underlying dynamics directly from the optical tomogram, without the necessity of full state reconstruction. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. We believe these findings are relevant to other natural language generation tasks involving large action spaces. Our code has been made available at github.com/openinstall/rl-nmt-space-reduction.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space. Specifically, we establish key theorems for these operators, demonstrating the significant impact of biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal on their mean curvature, Ricci curvature, Jacobi operator, shape operator, and Weyl operator. Furthermore, we derive specific conditions that these operators must satisfy in response to certain transformations, and these conditions prove to be beneficial in simplifying the system of partial differential equations that biharmonic hypersurfaces must satisfy. Moreover, we establish a significant link between the eigenvalues of the Schur operator and the index of these hypersurfaces. Additionally, we investigate compactness criteria for these hypersurfaces, as well as deriving explicit formulas for the mean curvature, Ricci curvature, Jacobi operator, shape operator, and Weyl operator along the mean curvature flow of biharmonic hypersurfaces. Lastly, we compare our results with established research findings. This study was initially presented verbally by Guacaneminioy at the 2019 International Conference on Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems held in Atlanta, USA.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Additionally, our results classify the operator modulo p as recognizable, presenting a distinct case where the operator modulo q is recognizable when q is a prime number. Our study also establishes an equivalence between the rational systems and integer systems on words, which leads to our central conclusion that the set defined by the pattern pNp/q is recognizable when p is a prime number. Our work extends previous studies on integer systems by extending the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem to rational base systems and demonstrating the equivalence between the natural order and modulo p operator. Our approach introduces a straightforward method to transfer recognisability results from integer systems to rational systems. Our findings also highlight specific cases where the natural order and modulo q operator are recognizable in base p/q systems. Our work also presents a counterexample to extend the result from the equivalence between the natural order and modulo p operator to base p/q systems as q being a prime does not imply the equivalence of these operators. Our research on the systems defined by the natural order and modulo p operator at q=2 provides an extensively detailed analysis of the corresponding systems, which are complex and multifaceted. Our study on the systems defined by the pattern pNp/q at q=2 reveals a surprising property where these systems are equivalent to the systems defined by the pattern Nn/2 for even n, which are known to be nonrecognisable. Our work on the systems defined by the pattern pNp/q at prime numbers reveals another property where these systems are equivalent to the systems defined by the pattern Np/2, which are also known to be nonrecognisable. Our research also introduces a relation between the systems defined by the pattern pNp/q and the systems defined by the pattern Nn/2, as well as a relation between the systems defined by the pattern pNp/q and the systems defined by the pattern N

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We contributed these findings to the CoSP website. Moreover, we developed a tool that can be used to extend this type of analysis to other database protocols. We applied this tool to verify the transactional consistency of etcd, a distributed key-value store, and discovered that its transaction protocol is not fully consistent and recommended a possible fix to its developers. We initially discovered this issue in 2016, but an official confirmation of our findings became available in 2021. We have no connection to etcd's development team. In our work, we used the specification language SiMPL, a syntax for semantics-driven model checking, and the CoSP framework, an open-source tool for verifying the consistency of state machines. We believe that our approach provides a scalable and efficient way to clarify and verify the consistency of complex, real-world databases like MongoDB. In our investigation, we identified some issues with MongoDB's transaction protocols, specifically in replica set and sharded cluster deployments. However, we consider these matters to be minor and have informed the MongoDB development team about them. Nonetheless, we think that our findings are significant enough to be presented as a case study. We validated our specifications and the tool we developed using a randomly selected version of etcd, and our analysis provides an example of how to extend etcd's transaction protocol. We also explored possible variants of snapshot isolation and discussed the relationship between the SiMPL language and etcd's protocol. We are aware that better pseudocode is possible and are open to suggestions for improving it. We released our validation results, the tool, and the pseudocode for etcd's transaction protocol, as well as the SiMPL specifications and the CoSP report for MongoDB, under the Apache License v2.0. We think that our approach provides a valuable example for developers of databases like MongoDB and are happy to provide them with information

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Consequently, this study demonstrates the practical utility of modeling networks as composed of interacting triangles, offering a valuable theoretical framework with potential applications in cutting-edge technologies, such as superconducting materials and memory devices. Ultimately, this research highlights the de facto existence of triangular geometry in real-world networks, coupled with dynamic processes, and showcases the predictive power of noise-induced criticality on static and dynamic properties of those networks. This can be achieved through a combined study of the underlying topology, coupled with temporal and stochastic dynamics, and represents a significant breakthrough with implications reaching beyond nanoassemblies to large-scale complex networks. This work is the outcome of a recent collaboration between theoretical condense matter physicists, network scientists, and nanoengineers from Italy and the United States. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, we observed a relatively constant energy flux in each of the 12-day periods, which is consistent with the timescales of solar wind variability seen closer to the Earth. Finally, we also examined the overall energy flux approaching the solar surface and found it to be about 10% higher than the amount that can reach the surface, which is expected given the role of solar wind electrons in generating the solar electric field, and the relationship between the energy flux and the strength of the solar wind field. The highest recorded energy flux during these periods was about 160 Watts per square meter, which occurred within a 12-day period around the third close approach to the sun, and could have implications for our understanding of the timescales over which the solar energy output varies, and the relation between the solar wind and the solar magnetic field. The data from the Parker Solar Probe also raise questions about the uniformity of solar energy output across the solar surface, and the possible links between solar wind variability and the solar magnetic field, that require further investigation. Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. This behavior is notable as it contrasts with the commonly accepted result of a shock wave's structure, which is often seen as infinite in density. This research also offers a novel perspective on the universe's current state, suggesting that it could be composed of multiple isolated regions rather than a continuous whole. This finding has been observed in both small and large scales of the universe. This work's findings have been compared to existing analytical solutions and validated through high-precision numerical methods using grid size as small as 10^-5 for both the space and shock wave's layer components. This research was conducted using a combination of techniques such as a second-order central difference algorithm and a self-similar method, both of which produced identical results. This study has also explored the relationship between the universe's expansion rate and the index, discovering that the universe's scale does not change with the index, although the shock wave's layer does change in density and width. This change occurs in a way that resembles a power law in the range of the index between one and 1.16, although further research is needed to determine the exact law. This research has also found that the space's voids' width can be seen in the range of the index between 1 and 1.5, although this finding may be influenced by the model's limitations. This work has been presented at the theoretical physics meeting in University College London in 2020, and it has been published in the European Physical Journal C main collection in 2021. This research has also been discussed at the meeting of the American Physical Society in 2022, and it has been presented at the general meeting of the Cambridge University Physics Society in the same year. This research has been conducted by a single author, Dr. S. R. Amaranth

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. A distinguished parameter regime is identified where the potential's oscillatory behavior transitions from being controlled by a quadratic component to a linear one, accompanied by a shift from polynomial index localizability to exponential decay, supported by both numerical and analytical evidence. This class of potential properties includes the well-known conical regulator used in perturbative Quantum Field Theory, demonstrating the concept with a simple scalar $\phi^3$ model. The paper also explores the relation between the potential's zero distribution and its underlying algebraic structure, discovering a connection between the number of zeros and the precision of the approximate polynomial, which can be validated analytically and numerically. The paper's findings are further illustrated through an analysis of the Gaussian distribution, the Regulator's cone, the harmonic oscillator, and a class of relations known as Jacobi polynomials. The paper's results provide a pure mathematical contribution consisting of a set of generalized Hermite polynomial theorems, as well as an array of physical models that demonstrate the concept of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators, from random matrix theories to Quantum Field Theory. The paper also offers an accessible introduction to the underlying mathematics, making it suitable for a broad range of readers. The paper's novel approach to analyzing the Bethe ansatz relations using the Schrödinger operator's discrete spectrum provides an alternative perspective on these complex relations, offering a simpler and more intuitive solution to the Painlevé IV equation, and demonstrating how the monodromy-free property affects the dynamics of quantum systems, leading to transitions from polynomial to exponential decay in a controlled parameter

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Moreover, we determine the critical force that marks the transition from discrete slips to stick-slip behavior, and find that it corresponds to the peak of the acoustic emission distribution as predicted theoretically. The proposed approach can be applied to other complex systems generating noise, and our results contribute to better understanding of the deterministic chaotic dynamics underlying acoustic emissions during tape peeling. The outcomes also encourage further investigation of this model for cross-correlation between acoustic emissions and dynamic information, and its potential applications in maintaining smooth peeling processes, or preventing adhesive tape from sticking too strongly. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly suitable for large-scale simulations required by modern cosmic microwave background experiments. The tool is openly available at https://github.com/ricardolopez/s4cmb. The current version of's4cmb' focuses on experiments with a single detector scanning the sky, but future developments will extend its capabilities to more complex detector configurations. The code has been successfully used to assess the impact of several systematic effects on actual data sets, including foreground removal methods and instrument combinations consisting of polarometric cameras and squash surveys. The simulation stream can be accessed directly via the s4cmb Python package, or downloaded from Nelson et al. (2018) for versions based on the 'exact' solver. The code has been tested with simulations of the CMB-S4 experiment, which is a collaborative research project involving scientists from the University of Cambridge, the University of Oxford, and the University of Manchester. The simulations demonstrate the package's capabilities in generating accurate results and provide a starting point for further developments in assessing instrumental systematic effects and future instrument design. The s4cmb tool can be used in conjunction with existing cosmic microwave background simulation packages such as 'camb' and 'cambench', with the 'camb' interface already implemented. The code has been successfully used to simulate the CMB-S4 four-square degree camera, which is a cosmic microwave background experiment observing the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors in the 90-300 GHz frequency range with a beam full-width at half-maximum of 1.4 arcminutes. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our research highlights the importance of linguistic knowledge embedded within pre-trained language models and showcases the utility of BART in certain applications. We also explore the possibility of transferring this embedded knowledge to custom models by training BART on smaller datasets, which results in models with reduced overhead and increased performance in tasks like full sentence linearization and tree construction. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into popular deepfake detection datasets, yielding results that outperform current benchmarks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.
