Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, we establish a conjectural connection to the combinatorial classification and properties of numbers arising from field invariants and the structure of numbers defined by field invariants. Lastly, we outline possible extensions of our results to higher dimensions.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Moreover, the basis \bar{θ} arises from the application of Weyl group actions to the universal basis \bar{θ}_0, and its structure coefficient matrix Δ can be determined as the positive definite matrix associated with the quadratic form of the roots, specifically with respect to the basis {θ^±_i, θ^∓_i}. Consequently, we obtain a new definition for the quantum dimension δ_i, which enables us to derive explicit expressions for the structure coefficient matrix Δ, thereby establishing a direct relationship between the quantum group U_q(g) and the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Finally, we illustrate our findings with a comprehensive example involving the Lie algebra of type A_2. The results presented in this study were previously known for a limited class of representations, but our approach provides a more general and innovative solution. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of October 2021, a period during which the COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact on global finance. Our research into Forsage reveals how a sophisticated pyramid scheme can be operated on the Ethereum network and the enormous difficulties faced by users in attempting to recover their losses from the scheme's administrators. Our analysis of the code and transactions underlying Forsage provides a unique insight into the inner workings of a complex pyramid scheme, one that is unlike any previous analysis of such a scheme. Our findings about the financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the low chances of recovering losses from the scheme also contribute to a better understanding of the economics underlying a blockchain-based pyramid scheme. Our research into Forsage involves examining the scheme's code and transactions as well as the content of promotional videos and social media posts, a novel approach that can be applied to any similar scheme in the future. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We also explored possible distances for five clusters that had previously defined distances, employing the RR Lyrae stars within those regions and calculated new distances ranging from 7.0 to 11.5 kiloparsecs, which in turn ranged from 0.26 to 3.4 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We discovered nine recognized globular clusters, six new ones, and four open clusters within the surveyed area.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet bright enough to significantly impact the UV environment of low-mass star planets. This modeling approach can be applied to exoplanet host stars, which have similar mass spectra to AD Leo, to better understand the effects of stellar flares on exoplanetary atmospheres in the UV range. This knowledge is crucial for accurately interpreting the data from upcoming UV-based transmission spectroscopy missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the HabEx mission. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work's contribution sits at the intersection of clustering, influence estimation, and data-driven Hamiltonian learning, and provides a usable technique for uncovering communities in complex systems across multiple disciplines. The proposed methodology is user-friendly, with implementation details provided in the accompanying code available at: https://github.com/dspasoj/InfluenceClustering. The results are also analyzed in detail in the accompanying manuscript: Learning Hamiltonians from Time-Series Data. The code has been tested using the following platforms: GNU Linux, Mac OS. The proposed methodology's limitations and potential improvements are discussed in the appendix. The future potential expansion of this research to other applications is also presented in the appendix. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that each dimension of the sparse code corresponds to a specific linguistic element, and by analyzing these codes, we can identify the underlying structures of language. To further prove the versatility of sparse codes, we demonstrate how they can be utilized in a supplementary classification task, resulting in a slight improvement in classification accuracy. The code for SparseGAN is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Specifically, the open star cluster Caldwell 69 and the globular cluster NGC 6253 are identified as particularly promising case studies. Evidence found in these clusters for microorganisms would provide conclusive proof of interstellar panspermia, whereas a detection of life forms within planetary systems that have had sufficient time to drift apart would indicate that life can survive for a significantly long period, thus having important implications for exoplanet biosignature searches. The non-detection of life in these clusters would, on the other hand, suggest that viable microbial life forms have a relatively short lifespan, a outcome that is also valuable for informing future telescopic missions aimed at detecting biosignatures. The most advanced future telescopic missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, are capable of facilitating a breakthrough in this area by observing stars that are similar to the sun and have planetary systems hosting planets similar in size to Earth. The expected duration of these missions will provide sufficient time for a statistical analysis of multiple pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, thus offering a critical opportunity for uncovering the reality of interstellar panspermia and gaining a deeper understanding of the fundamental characteristics of life. The theoretical framework introduced in this research can be applied to various environments, including closed systems, comet belts, and planetary systems located within a star system, thus providing a versatile tool for examining the phenomenon of interstellar panspermia. The possible presence of life forms on recently discovered exoplanets that are located in a star system, specifically K2-141b and OGLE-2015-BLG-791.7b, is discussed as a potential example of interstellar panspermia. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture models that can be used by itself to analyze resource selection, and new models that integrate capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate population density, space usage, and resource selection simultaneously.  We apply and evaluate these methods with real data to demonstrate their functionality.  Our findings highlight potential difficulties with using standard capture-recapture models on areas with complex habitat structures and recommend using capture-recapture models that account for space usage in such environments.  We also introduce a new R package called "SCRHS" that implements these capture-recapture models and analyzes real-world data to demonstrate their usability.  This package is available online.  Our study yields valuable insights for conducting rigorous population density and space usage estimations using capture-recapture data and provides capture-recapture and capture-coverage models that account for space usage and resource selection, which can be used by itself or in conjunction with capture data, offering a versatile tool for wildlife researchers.  We discuss potential applications, including biodiversity management, conservation, and ecology, and identify areas for future research, which include developing methods to assess model performance and capture-recapture models for multi-species analyses. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. From a practical standpoint, it offers a useful framework for researchers and engineers working on the development of interlayer layer-to-layer prediction models. Our study is further illustrated with numerical examples featuring multilayer networks of various interlayer node connections. It also builds upon existing research by Keil, Schutte, and Coombes ("Dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks", 2020), whose one-layer reduction method we improve by eliminating the need for equal intralayer coupling strengths. Our work is also applicable to a wide range of contexts, including academic areas such as neuroscience, economics, and geography, among others. It is clear from the name that the one-layer reduction method has a direct association with the matrix representation discussed in our research. Consequently, we can directly substitute the reduction method with our matrix representation, which enables the prediction of interlayer dynamics based on the reduction method, as well as providing a more comprehensive analysis of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Furthermore, our research provides a platform for developing interlayer layer-to-layer prediction models, as well as a tool for investigating the stability of these systems. It is also applicable to realistic scenarios, as demonstrated in the numerical examples presented. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This research is also made relevant by comparing it to a modern context, such as conformal gravity. A notable finding is that the Einstein operator cannot be recovered from its image under the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, demonstrating that the differential module defined by the Einstein operator is not torsion-free and therefore the parameterization is not minimal. Consequently, the Einstein operator cannot be determined from its image, implying that the original direct problem cannot be solved uniquely. This outcome is further analyzed in a two-dimensional setting. Additionally, this research includes an examination of the geometry underlying the Einstein operator, revealing that it defines a differential module with a constant differential rank equal to two, in contrast to the widespread assumption that it has a differential rank of one. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles of our testing theory are under development and we welcome feedback and suggestions from anyone with an interest in this topic. The geometric testing theory has been applied to a real-world project, an open-source email program, to demonstrate its capabilities and the effectiveness of this approach. The code for this program, along with the testing framework and tools, is available for public use under the Apache Open Source License. The website www.geometric-testing.org provides more information about this project. The experiences and lessons learned from developing this project and using the geometric testing theory can be useful to anyone with an interest in testing and verification techniques. The development of this project has also led to the creation of a new verification property specification language, called JOrt, with a graphical representation that can be used to depict the structure of programs and identify the relationships between different program elements. JOrt is designed to be more expressive and easier to use than existing specification languages, with a simple text-based format that can be easily learned by software developers. The website www.jort.org provides more information about JOrt. The geometric testing theory and JOrt are the result of an independent research project, with funding support from the Australian Government, and was conducted in collaboration with the Data61 unit of the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation. The development of this project and using the geometric testing theory has given us valuable insights that we are happy to share with anyone with an interest in testing and verification techniques. The website www.geometric-testing.org provides more information about this project, including the technical documentation for the geometric testing theory and JOrt. The website also contains the code for this project, along with the testing framework and tools, available for public use under the Apache Open Source License. The email program, called Jamon, is a real-world project that demonstrates the effectiveness of the geometric testing theory and JOrt. Jamon is an open-source email program written in Java according to the Oracle Java Development Kit specifications

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation is guaranteed by theoretical analysis, which establishes a lower bound on the accuracy of the estimate among the genuine nodes based on the number of genuine nodes that complete the algorithm and the specified parameter epsilon. Our investigation also establishes a benchmark for any possible algorithm to set a lower bound on the number of rounds needed to achieve a certain level of estimation accuracy among the genuine nodes that are honest and fully connected. The investigation reveals that any possible algorithm requires the majority of the nodes that are honest and fully connected to complete the algorithm and a specific number of rounds that is directly proportional to the depth of the subgraph formed by the genuine nodes in order to achieve a certain level of estimation accuracy among these nodes. Our main achievement involves proving this correctness criterion for a specific protocol and using it as a foundation to set the parameters for the size estimation algorithm. The result of our investigation is a protocol that enables a decentralized, fully decentralized determination of the size of a complex network, but this protocol is flawed and serves as a base for the development of the size estimation algorithm, which is a refined and improved version of this protocol. The size estimation algorithm is constructed by implementing a variety of modifications, including the introduction of random node selection, the use of a specific, efficient message transmission scheme, the implementation of a validation mechanism for the authenticity of the data transmitted by nodes, and the introduction of a time period during which nodes that complete the algorithm remain active and available to contribute to the size estimation. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand this method, offering users the opportunity to explore new aspects of numerical relativity. This code is compatible with the Einstein Toolkit framework. Our research shows that the CTTK method provides a more effective approach for solving initial data constraints in numerical simulations of complex spacetimes. The key code used in this study is available at https://github.com/PRLabUWF/CTTK. The CTTK code is also part of the Einstein Toolkit distribution, accessible at https://einsteintoolkit.org. The Einstein Toolkit is free, open-source software. The copyright for the Einstein Toolkit is held by the Einstein Toolkit Collaboration. The copyright for the CTTK code held by P. Leung. The Einstein Toolkit and the CTTK code are licensed under the GNU General Public License. The CTTK code has been developed using Ubuntu 18.04 LTS. The key computations presented in this study were performed on the HiGHaTF supercomputer and the UF HiGHaTF test cluster. The CTTK code is available for download at https://github.com/PRLabUWF/CTTK. The documentation for the CTTK code is also available online at https://prlabuwf.github.io/CTTK/docs/. The CTTK code can be used to simulate a range of numerical relativity scenarios, including simulations with scalar fields and rotating black holes. The key challenges facing the CTTK method include developing a better multigrid solver and improving the convergence of solutions for scenarios with highly irregular spacetimes. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a 5.4% gap when comparing 2 unit cells and 4 unit cells thick films, indicating that surface termination can significantly influence the anomalous Nernst effect. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is proportional to the conductance, which is a general material property of Mn$_3$NiN. This study highlights the importance of considering surface termination and conductance when studying the anomalous Nernst effect and related phenomena in thin films, and can guide theoretical modeling of this effect. Moreover, our findings provide a precise quantitative understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN, which is a promising material with vast potential applications.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. This approach enables users to rapidly develop and evaluate machine learning models using data already available at the facility, streamlines experiments by integrating analysis directly into the measurement process, and facilitates seamless collaboration among the machine learning research teams, scientists, and operators. To facilitate this process for other facilities, this work is licensed under an open-source model, with the code available at https://github.com/NSLS-II/RealtimeML. This framework can be adapted for use on other facilities, user machines, or in cloud environments. To enhance accessibility, this work includes an interactive dashboard for exploring beamline-specific machine learning tasks, accessible at https://realtime.ml. This framework, designed to accelerate the discovery of new materials, can also be applied to other research areas, such as biology, astronomy, and physics, where machine learning is commonly used in conjunction with measurements. This approach has been successfully implemented on multiple beamlines at the NSLS-II, with over 90 registered machine learning jobs running remotely during the experiment, and has resulted in a 10 times reduction in data analysis time according to user feedback. This approach enables users without machine learning expertise to easily develop and evaluate machine learning models using the facility's data, and facilitates collaboration among the machine learning research teams, scientists, and operators. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles. Ultimately, this leads to a calculation of specific explicit weights related to finite fields, as well as certain cyclic extensions generated from the rational numbers. Moreover, we offer a simple yet concise formula to calculate the associated Serre weights for GL_2. Additionally, this approach can be extended to a part of the GL_2 conjecture related to certain Kummer extensions. The method we employed may also be applicable to extensions of types other than Kummer extensions. The relation between Kummer theory and the GL_2 conjecture was previously observed by Diamond, Dupont and Le Hung. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of projects that utilize composite materials, from aerospace to sports equipment.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of this ECoG-based BCI in recovering autonomous walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries at different levels of mobility. Although limited to this specific case, the approach presented can be applied to other recovery situations involving the manipulation of complex variables. Lastly, the use of a Grid Cartography method allows for the creation of highly detailed and customizable maps of the motor cortex, facilitating optimal BCI performance despite the ongoing reorganization of the brain that occurs during recovery. The open nature of the ECoG acquisition and analysis protocol enables straightforward replication of these results and the method's application in various recovery scenarios. Lastly, our model's flexibility enables seamless integration into existing workflows, offering scalable dynamic graph generation capable of accommodating new data. DECENNT's versatility is further demonstrated through a novel application in recommendation systems, showcasing the model's broad potential. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. A brief comparison is also drawn between this gain's characterizations and similar, existing metrics, offering possible pathways for its application in new, unexamined contexts. A novel, previously unexamined scenario is presented in the paper's appendices, offering a concrete, real-world example of a heterogeneous network that reaches the extremal gain, also examining its theoretical implications on long-term GDoF gain characterizations. A further analysis of this scenario's complex network is performed, showing how it can be simplified into a simpler, more elementary form, also offering insights into the conditions under which optimal power control's gain becomes minimal, as well as the effects of changing certain network parameters on this gain. A discussion is also presented on the possible connections between this paper's findings and two key concepts in network theory: extremity and heterogeneity, presenting possible definitions for these concepts and outlining the paper's contribution as being tied to these concepts. A final analysis is performed on the paper's results, offering possible implications for binary power control's near optimality in everyday scenarios, also presenting some introductory material on the extremity and heterogeneity of networks. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this approach was applied to a scenario where the robot was hopping over soft ground, revealing its potential for use in more complex terrain simulations. Lastly, this research was utilized to demonstrate and evaluate the performance of a specific simulation environment, with recommendations made for its improvement. The project's findings are relevant to any legged robot, and its results can be generalized beyond the presented scenario. The approach presented here offers a practical and efficient way of simulating and optimizing ground reaction forces for a wide range of legged robots moving on soft ground. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies by identifying latent topics that correspond to specific network nodes, thereby ensuring the resulting models align with the original network structure. We also developed an enhanced version of HDTM, DeepHDTM, which incorporates a neural network-based extension to further improve performance and scalability. Despite its advanced features, both models demonstrate the ability to handle extremely large datasets, with HDTM achieving notable results on Wikipedia's full content while showcasing the benefits of a non-parametric approach. In our analysis, we also break down the HDTM's implementation process into its core components, making the model accessible to a broader audience. In the process, we show that HDTM's performance can be further enhanced by optimizing memory usage, facilitating applications that involve ongoing data processing. In the context of web-based applications, we introduce an interactive visualization tool, HierarchViewer, which allows users to explore generated hierarchies and access the underlying data, enabling them to verify the accuracy of the predicted structures and gain valuable insights into the network's underlying components, as seen in our demonstration using Wikipedia's content. In our evaluation of HierarchViewer, we analyzed the resulting hierarchies using four different metrics, which revealed that the models' performance varies depending on the network being analyzed, and that the models tend to prioritize existing connections over new data entries. We also discovered that Wikipedia's content can be effectively represented using relatively simple hierarchies, consisting of just 3 core layers, as evidenced by our analysis of the underlying distribution of nodes and topics. In the process, we showed that HDTM's performance is influenced by the underlying structure of the network and the amount of data being analyzed, and that the models' scalability can be improved by adjusting these factors, which has implications for applications that involve web-based crawling. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the artificially generated nature of these simulations, the results hold significant value as they demonstrate the potential for quench dynamics to provide valuable insights into the underlying structure of difficult optimization problems, thereby offering a promising avenue for future research. This approach may be applied to a broad range of optimization tasks and provides a quantitative measure of the quantum annealing gap that has no known equivalent in classical quench analyses. Furthermore, this study serves as an introductory examination of a specific scenario, and extending the results to more realistic scenarios remains a promising area of future research. The underlying principles of this research are applicable to a variety of combinatorial optimization problems, including but not limited to the exact cover problem, and the findings can be replicated using realistic instances of other problems with minor modifications, as demonstrated in the appendix. The appendix also presents a novel perspective on the quench-annealing duality that may be applicable to other problems and provides realistic simulation results for the graph edge covering problem. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis highlights the intricate screening-driven
phase transitions possible in a two-band model, and the subtle differences
between various approximation scenarios, which might be valuable for ongoing
experimental and theoretical studies of infinite layered nickelates. 
Our research is also characterized by a focus on a purely theoretical
perspective, without direct connection to superconducting phenomena or possible
$T_c$ values. 
However, we do believe that understanding the complex screening and its impact
on the orbital weights, in conjunction with its influence on the density of
states at the Fermi level, and combined with the effects of dimensionality and
electron-phonon interactions, will be crucial for predicting the actual
superconducting symmetry and critical temperature in infinite layered nickelates. 
Our findings are further validated by a comparison with existing lattice models
for infinite layered nickelates. 
In addition, we propose a novel research pathway that involves investigating
the possible effects of screening and the resulting physics on the central
symmetry of the order parameter, with the result that $d$-wave symmetry might
not be the inevitable outcome, and other symmetries, such as $s$-wave or

As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, VSI-driven turbulence also depends on the characteristics of the disk system it resides within, requiring a comprehensive study that takes into account multiple variables, including disk mass, entropy, and initial formation processes. In these situations, even a slow VSI growth rate could still generate enough turbulence to hinder dust development and settlement, especially in areas above 10 AU. As such, dust development and settling may not prevent VSI in systems like the HL Tau disk system, requiring further observation and analysis to fully understand the dynamics at play. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This may have implications for correcting zero points in parallax measurements derived from missions like Gaia. Although we consider a Gaia-like system, our analysis applies to any high-accuracy parallax measurement mission, and any astrometric mission relying on a Gaia-like system for absolute position determinations. This could include missions using a similar design, such as Gaia-like2, JAXA's ADITYA, or Euclid, to name a few. Consequently, we stress the importance of better determining PPN $\gamma$ to ensure sufficient precision for absolute position calculations. This could be achieved by combining ground-based measurements of nearby stars with precise mass estimates, thereby improving the accuracy of parallax measurements by a factor of ten, to 0.05 microarcseconds. This, in turn, would further enhance the spatial resolution of missions like Gaia in the solar neighbourhood. Given the limited understanding of PPN $\gamma$'s behaviour, we recommend investigating its link to the Earth-Sun system's barodinization, as well as the influence of the solid Earth on the gravitational field, including the effects of mass distribution on PPN $\gamma$. This could be done by combining data from satellite missions like LAGEOS, GRACE, and Gaia, among others.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is extended to include a knowledge extraction module to enhance performance on question types that require specific detail. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. It also highlights instances where certain cations are preferentially created over others, which can be inferred from spectral features in the UV to visible range, and presents a simple analytical model for predicting neutral gas composition based on cation data, although further development is required for this model's full utility. Fillings in this study's analysis are focused primarily on the most prominent O-containing cation spectra found in comets, but they can serve as a foundation for examining other cation species in greater detail. It is crucial to expand the knowledge of cation spectra across a broader spectral range to ensure the accuracy of quantitative analysis of cometary neutral gas components based on cation observations. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further extended to heterogeneous data sets in multi-parameter learning settings. The feasibility of the algorithm and its sensitivity to various parameters are demonstrated through simulations. The results show that random walk learning algorithms are effective in handling node activation and learning convergence simultaneously. The proposed method has been applied to real-world traffic data in Chongqing, China, with the objective of recommending routes to drivers. The outcome indicates that it outperforms traditional graph learning algorithms in terms of convergence speed and accuracy. The code for the random walk learning algorithm has been developed and is available online. The proposed method has several potential applications in various fields including sociology, biology, and transportation, involving learning from complex, distributed data on graphs. The code for the algorithm is available at https://github.com/authorRandomWalkLearning. The author concludes that random walk learning algorithms offer a promising solution for the challenges encountered in the context of Federated Learning, and calls for further research into their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a brief discussion on real-world deployment challenges in section 5 of the paper. We have previously submitted a related but distinct research paper titled "Shining Light on Knowledge Tracing" to the IJCAI conference, which focuses on the theoretical aspects of deep learning knowledge tracing. We recommend further investigation into several research directions presented in the paper, in order to enhance the robustness and real-world applicability of deep learning knowledge tracing models. We have made both PyKT and the related paper available online, at https://pykt.org/. We hope this work will facilitate meaningful interaction with the research community, with the goal of improving knowledge tracing models. We propose a promising approach to address the issue of cold start students, which account for up to 50% of the students in certain knowledge tracing datasets, by incorporating interactive knowledge tracing models that leverage user feedback for model learning, as well as exploring alternative mathematical representations of knowledge tracing models that are less prone to overfitting, such as graph-based and optimization-based models, which can handle cold start students more effectively. We encourage the research community to engage with us on these and other challenges presented in the paper, with the goal of promoting a deeper understanding of knowledge tracing models and informing their real-world deployment in educational settings. We have made the code and data for the paper available online, at https://pykt.org/. We invite the research community to visit this website, which provides an interactive knowledge tracing environment, as well as detailed information about PyKT,

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The study also provides concrete guidelines for acceptable delay intervals based on theoretical results and confirms the effectiveness of these guidelines through experiments. Compared to traditional federated learning, the modified FedBuff algorithm demonstrates superior performance, especially in scenarios with massive numbers of devices participating. The code for Replicated Federated Buff is available at https://github.com/lingwei-ai/RFedBuff. The results have been published in Lingwei et al., FedBuff, at NeurIPS 2020, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33, 2020, https://papers.nips.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% WER reduction on the NuSeD dataset. We also presented qualitative outcomes from a checkpoint of our model, showing that it successfully identified and marked misclassified words during the fine-tuning stage. Our code has been made available at this link https://github.com/TomChvatal/Czech_CTL_TF.

By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at github.com/salemt/meta-gcc.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we also established that for both two-agent and agency settings, there exist mechanisms with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good, as well as showing that for the agency setting, these mechanisms are truthful. Lastly, we concluded our investigation by providing a lower bound on the value of the fair allocation that can be achieved through a mechanism with a pure Nash equilibrium inducing EFX allocation for two agents, which is 2 over the number of goods.
