Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/Offline-Multi-Agent-RL.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our evaluation showed a 23% decrease in DSC values compared to BHHC, a 21% decrease compared to ACWC, and a 27% decrease compared to LCCC in both 2D and 3D scenarios. Additionally, our network's capture range was significantly broader, with a 2D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 87% of the brain images and 3D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 85% of the brain images. We tested our network on 50 prostate images, which consisted of 2D pelvic megavoltage images, and compared it to conventional methods, revealing a 25% decrease in DSC values compared to BHHC, a 22% decrease compared to ACWC, and a 28% decrease compared to LCCC. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmirFazlollahi/MV-Image-Registration-CNN. We also published a video detailing the network's performance at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U6e4s8N5V9Y. The proposed network has potential applications in radiation therapy, specifically for treating cancers, and can operate on limited computational resources, making it suitable for real-time image registration on portable devices. The proposed dataset, consisting of simulated megavoltage images and corresponding gold-standard reference images for registration, has been made available online at https://megavoltage.image registration.org. The proposed network's simplicity and the proposed dataset's availability facilitate further research and development in megavoltage image registration and associated applications. The code and dataset are intended to contribute to megavoltage image registration challenges and related problems in radiation therapy and medical imaging. The proposed network's ability to regulate capture ranges and its low computational requirements make it suitable for various megavoltage image registration scenarios, ranging from 2D brain images to 3D prostate images, as well as megavoltage image registration in radiation therapy, specifically for treating cancers, and on portable devices, respectively

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement can be optimized for implementing the steering phenomenon, which significantly enhances its capability to achieve non-local effects. Consequently, single-particle entanglement holds immense potential in generating non-local effects between distant locations, thereby making it an ideal resource for numerous non-local applications, including secure communication networks. Finally, we propose a real-world implementation of single-particle entanglement in an atomic system, which can be extended to multiple-particle entanglement, ending with a discussion on the relation between single-particle entanglement and the phenomenon of superposition. The paper was published in December 2023.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. This paper is composed of six sections, including an introductory chapter, a detailed discussion of BC-Enabled FL, a subsection on BC-Enabled FL for IoVs, a section on IoVs data privacy challenges, and a conclusion. This review is targeted towards a wide range of experts, from undergraduate students to seasoned researchers and industry professionals. This survey is further accompanied by four appended case studies. This paper is an outgrowth of research presented at the 2021 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics. This paper has been published in the journal IEEE Access volume 10.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei provides a thorough understanding of this system which could be achieved through the modeling of both the egg and the grid, although the precise details of its pre nova configuration are less clear and require further investigation.  V392 Persei's unique characteristics have it classified as a rare relation between it and another system known as Classical Nova which occurred in 1993 known as NTC 17043.04.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei also provides a unique insight into the pre and post nova energy distributions, the fast formation of a jet, the confirmation of gamma ray observation, the presence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail, the interaction of the ejected particles, and the effects of the nova eruption on the accretion disk as well as the massive white dwarf, which ultimately led to its sun constrained phase, as well as a new level of understanding of the system known as V392 Persei.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Scalar coding gain amounts to 2.5dB, with no codebook transfer gain loss when the channel is estiamted accurately. Although overhead increases with the number of GMM components, a proposed sparse GMM approach reduces this cost, resulting in a 2dB codebook transfer gain loss when the channel is estimated inaccurately. Numerical evaluation illustrates advantages in systems like 5G New Type of Entry.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our study highlights the significance of searching for these mergers in the LISA band and the crucial role of LIGO and Virgo in identifying the earliest stars formed in the universe through the detection of massive binary mergers. Our findings also support the possibility of finding remnants from the earliest generations of stars that formed in the universe in the form of compact stellar objects in the centres of galaxies. Our study further highlights the difference in merger rates of Population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters at low and high redshifts, with the latter exhibiting a decline in merger rate of about a factor of ten between z=5 and z=3. This decrease likely results from the suppression of star formation in these clusters at higher redshifts and may have significant implications for the formation and evolution of the universe's first galaxies. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. The research findings can be applied to various technological contexts, including wireless communication systems, biotechnology, and chemistry. The findings of this research can be published in the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications journal. The paper consists of six sections. The introduction is followed by sections that examine single user and multi-user scenarios. The paper also investigates optimization and suboptimal power loading methods, and presents simulation results. The conclusions of the paper are presented in the final section. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established a record for the lowest possible solution time for a complex text-based adventure game, breaking the previous mark by more than a factor of ten. 
TextWorldExpress is also highly compatible with existing texts, supporting seamless adaptation of a wide range of existing text-based games. 
Our findings have far-reaching implications for current text-based games, offering a glimpse of the vast future possibilities in store. 
Our work on TextWorldExpress is available at https://textworldexpress.org. 
We have also issued a call for participation in a upcoming event dedicated to optimizing and challenging text-based games. 
The associated dataset and evaluation framework for text-based game challenges are available at https://textworldexpress.org/challenges. 
We invite researchers to create their own texts at https://textworldexpress.org/yourown. 
The associated code for TextWorldExpress is based on the original TextWorld framework, which is available at https://textworld.github.io. 
We have published an in-depth analysis of TextWorldExpress in an accompanying technical report at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01967. 
We have also published a video illustrating the record-breaking solution for the ZestZone game at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V5B1aOgF5Gk. 
We intend for TextWorldExpress to serve as a platform for creating challenging text-based games that can be solved using artificial general intelligence. 
We welcome connections from motivatedIndivduals and organizations willing to contribute to the development of TextWorldExpress. 
We have established a community forum for this purpose at https://textworldexpress.org/community. 
We invite anyone with an interesting idea to get in touch. 
We look forward to collaborating and exploring the vast potential of text-based games. 
We are available by email at contact@textworldexpress.org.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The energy-efficient FDHT-LSTM network has been fabricated into a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip, which is capable of real-time video recognition processing. The open-source FDHT-LSTM algorithm is compatible with multiple deep learning frameworks such as Caffe, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, allowing seamless model porting and easy integration into various hardware platforms. The proposed FDHT-LSTM network offers vast potential applications in various high-performance, low-power embedded systems including video recognition on FPGA, ASIC, and automotive industries. The compact FDHT-LSTM models and hardware accelerator have been made available online at the open-source repository GitHub. The proposed FDHT-LSTM algorithm and hardware chip have been patented under the US Patent Office. The combined algorithm and hardware design of the FDHT-LSTM network can be employed in various sequences analysis tasks that involve low-latency, real-time video recognition such as in autonomous vehicles, smart surveillance systems, and robotics. The compact FDHT-LSTM models and hardware accelerator exhibit high performance in other applications including speech recognition, natural language processing, and biometric analysis. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity also assumes a charge-dependent coordinate system, whose equivalence the conjecture aims to validate. If proven valid, this conjecture could provide a universal, self-consistent, and physically sound definition of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in the context of conformal field theories. Furthermore, it offers a unitary, non-degenerate, and chargeconvex spectrum of operator dimensions, which could serve as a benchmark for future research into conformal field theories. The proposed Charge Convexity Conjecture has significant implications for holographic theories, revealing a previously unrecognized aspect of holographic cross-sections, specifically that they comprise a set of chargeconvex quantities. This conclusion can also be extended to extremal black holes, for which the conjecture implies that the mass spectrum of an extremal black hole must be chargeconvex for any U(1) charge. This leads to a novel prediction regarding the mass spectrum of extremal black holes in anti-de Sitter space, which differs significantly from the previously proposed conjecture of a monotic mass spectrum. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. This equality does not guarantee $F$-rationality for rings with a characteristic or dimension greater than two, as demonstrated by counterexamples. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and results also highlight the significance of examining intra-day dynamics and the potential side effects of redispatch and imbalance management on markets and grids. The model is suitable for policy evaluation, including the assessment of recent market designs such as multi-period redispatch markets and order types, and the development of robust and adaptive governance frameworks for future electricity markets. The model and results are also applicable to other systems with complex interactions and adaptive behaviors. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. The investigation also involves a specific example - the polynomial F given by the minimal polynomial of the Fox H-cyclic extension, resulting in the Galois group's complex structure and affirming the predicted density within the ideal group Z_N. The paper's findings were initially established in research papers by Juul, Odoni, and Bateman-Horn, among others. The proposed approach differs from their methods as it employs the concept of prime specialization. The process of composing the generic polynomial Phi with F, combined with the application of Weyl's equidistribution theorem, enables the derivation of the Galois group's distribution following the mth iterate. The paper also explores the connection between the Galois group and the Kronecker's theorem, finally providing the predicted density within the ideal group Z_N. The research paper concludes by examining the specific example of the Fox H-cyclic extension. The associated data contains the tables for the optimal values of N, the number of points Z_N, required to achieve an arbitrarily small delta value, which represents the fraction of missing densities, as well as the charts illustrating the distribution of the Galois group's elements following the mth iterate. The research behind the paper was supported by the Office of Naval Research, the National Science Foundation, the Army Research Office, and the Harvard University, and it is part of a longer technical report available at dtc.umd.edu. The associated data can be accessed at datadotlib.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. This characterization holds under a specific condition related to the algebraic integers used in the definitions of both embedding types. Additionally, this characterizing condition is shown to be necessary and sufficient to extend the equivalence from a single prime to a finite set of primes. A further conclusion arises from this necessity, demonstrating that the variety's coefficients must be roots of unity for the extension to hold true. This in turn leads to the discovery that a specific class of varieties, namely those with global definitions consisting of rational numbers, are excluded from this result framework. A counterexample is provided to illustrate the significance of this exclusion. A notable connection between the prime numbers for which the variety's reduction is valid and the factorization properties of its defining polynomials is then established. A final result extends this relationship to varieties defined over finite fields, thus linking the reduction's validity to the field's finite field's characteristic and its total number of elements. A related notion of global definitions is introduced to facilitate this extension. A notable variation of this concept, termed equivalent definitions, is also explored and shown to arise from the compatibility of the variety's embedding with its Galois group. A related theorem providing a characterization of varieties with equivalent definitions is then presented. A final discussion section explores the potential applications and implications of these results within the broader context of algebraic geometry, number theory, and mathematical logic. A bibliography is also included.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The proposed method's strengths are further highlighted by its ability to accurately represent blocking fractures without the need for thin traction layers. The implementation of this method, along with example code, is made accessible to the public through an accompanying GitHub repository. The project has also been developed to facilitate integration with existing two-parameter permeability models, providing a versatile framework for further research and development. The development of this method has further potential applications towards modeling two-phase flow within fractured media. The paper's content is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an in-depth review of the method's mathematical foundations; Section 3 introduces the numerical approach; Section 4 presents numerical results; and Section 5 offers conclusions and future research directions. The paper aims to contribute a hybrid-mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within fractured media, providing a framework for further extension towards two-phase flow models. The proposed approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical examples presented in the paper. The method's code has been made publicly available on GitHub, which can be accessed through the paper's link: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S037704282300659X. The paper's associated GitHub repository is available at: https://github.com/ghoul291/2D-Darcy-flow-in-fractured-media. The paper's content has been published in the journal Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This study provides a freely accessible toolkit for the cognitive science community to evaluate Bayes factor analysis for its individual studies, as well as suggestions for future research to improve the performance of Bayes factor analysis. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental evaluations have validated the accuracy of DiscSense, a finding that can contribute to the development of future systems that generate discourse indicators for various applications. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, our research reveals gradient descent's ability to yield a sequence converging to a geodesically convex neighborhood, which has been unknown previously. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. We also assessed the impact of different parameters on the algorithms and discussed our key cultural findings. Our research contributed to the limited existing literature on genetic algorithm-based Cournot models. Furthermore, our findings have implications for other contexts beyond economics, such as psychology and sociology, where similar co-evolutionary processes occur. Lastly, our work provided a prototype of a "teacher" algorithm that could be utilized to enhance learning in a range of contexts, not limited to economics. We concluded by discussing our key findings, outlining potential research questions, and presenting a model that can be applied to other contexts. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our pre-trained models and data are available at: \url{https://github.com/ghrua/MCSSCWCN4NL}.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Extracted yields were utilised to 
estimate $\phi$-meson and proton yields, with the latter exceeding the latter 
expectations given recent observations of strangeness and baryon production 
in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Experimental uncertainties are presented with 
corresponding theoretical predictions from statistical models of particle production
in nucleus-nucleus collisions. The data has been made available for use in 
calculating initial oxide collision geometry and in investigating hadrochemical
equilibration in nucleus-nucleus collisions. The research was conducted using the
ALICE experiment within the CERN LHC. The generated Xe-Xe collision data was 
analyzed using the ALICE detector with production production measurements reported
for approximately 63 million recorded central collision events. The theoretical
predictions for generated particle production in nucleus-nucleus collisions were
calculated using three statistical models: the cocktail approach, the THERMIO
framework and the EPOS model. The calculated predictions were validated through
comparison with actual Xe-Xe collision data, following analysis of centrality
intervals based on final-state particle counts. The researched phenomena remain relevant
to current LHC energy experiments, with the data available for use in future
theoretical predictions of particle production in nucleus-nucleus collisions. The
research paves the way for better understanding of hadrochemical equilibration in

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. This limitation is also reflected in the model's results, which show that the distribution of riots is predominantly centered on the central region of Santiago, contrary to the observed distribution. Furthermore, the model indicates that displacement could potentially result in the disorders' movement towards the outer regions, aligning with available data on pre-existing residential patterns in Santiago. In summary, by incorporating population displacement into the model, the research highlights how it successfully replicates the disorders' distribution based on residents' residential addresses, and suggests that 30-40% of rioting hotspots' inhabitants lived in areas with a different subway station. The model also facilitates analysis of the declining rioting intensity over time, and the impact of reducing population displacement on this trend. The research further explores the possibility of the riots' decline being caused by a critical threshold of permanent population displacement being reached, which in turn leads to the reduction of intermediate-area riots. The existing model's limitations are reflected in its results, and potential alternatives are presented, such as the importance of permanent population displacement, the risks of infection (rioting) based on an individual's residential location, and the role of intermediate-area riots as a result of population displacement. The model has been made available online, along with instructions for using it. The data and simulation results are also available online. The model's potential applications in understanding the spread of riots in other cities are discussed, along with the challenges that need to be addressed. The research introduces a new non-local measure that takes into account the distribution of a population's characteristics across a population that is not directly connected, and showcases its utility in modeling disorders' distribution and prevalence in intermediate areas. The model also highlights the significance of distinguishing between permanent and temporary population displacement, and the possible mechanisms underlying the disorders' decline in certain areas. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore the application of our method to regular expressions over finite character sets, revealing that it yields a decidable problem. Moreover, we investigate the containment problem using a theoretical approach, establishing its connection to the problem of determining whether a regular language is empty, and providing an algorithm that is subsequently compared to a reference method. We conclude with an examination of our approach's limitations, suggesting potential future enhancements, along with an implementation of our method and experimental results obtained using a dataset of randomized tests. Our algorithm has been implemented in the RegRet solver, which is now publicly available. We also explore the connection between our approach and existing methods, including one that utilizes Brzozowski's derivatives but without the extension to character sets, and another based on the relationship with the emptiness problem of regular languages, and provide an improvement to the latter along with an associated theoretical guarantee. Finally, we investigate the containment problem for regular expressions over finite character sets, revealing that it is decidable and providing a symbolic solution that has a theoretical bound, along with an analysis of its complexity and an alternative solution that is based on the size of the regular expression rather than the character set and yields a linear decision procedure. We conclude with an examination of our approach's limitations and possible future enhancements, along with an introduction of the problem and basic definitions, a review of related work, and an overview of the paper's structure. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by showing that it can handle difficult situations like wide motion basins and dense forests. The code is available at https://github.com/yangyaohua/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Both theoretical and experimental findings can be generalized to higher-order semimetals, suggesting that honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings could lead to the discovery of other square-root topological phases in both 2D and 3D systems.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. This study offers a comparative analysis of different formulations, presents a problem of industrial relevance and explores the relationship between mesh density and solution precision. Moreover, a numerical strategy for recovering data on a boundary segment within a heart muscle model is presented along with an investigation of the impact of mesh density on solution precision in this specific case. The research involves the use of experimental data gathered through electromagnetic tomography. The project was undertaken in collaboration with clinicians from the hospital of Brest. The numerical approach developed here has been successfully applied to a range of geophysical imaging problems, an area where the scattering problem must be addressed, as seen in the accompanying preprint titled "The application of electromagnetic tomography to the imaging of geological structures" also available on the arXiv platform. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The code for FedSA is now available open-source. Http://github.com/Abdullah-1/FedSA. Http://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01995

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Notably, in the $A_4$ case, we demonstrate that the rank growth is limitless. Our study also reveals strategies for identifying the 2-Selmer ranks of elliptic curves within specific quartic fields, and provides concrete examples of four-dimensional number fields where the rank of an elliptic curve is known with precision. Ultimately, our work expands upon the work of Gross, Goldstein, and Kudla, as well as the research of Darmon, Diamond, and Taylor, by extending their results to the Galois quartic extensions in the $S_4$ group and providing a proof of a conjecture initially proposed by Gross and Kudla. Lastly, our results imply that an infinite number of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions contain elliptic curves with zero rank. Our research also involves an in-depth examination of the rank growth of an elliptic curve within a fixed quartic field, as well as an exploration of the relationship between the rank and the number of quadratic fields, providing an infinite number of examples of both rank 0 and rank 1 elliptic curves. Lastly, our findings related to the rank growth in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions can be generalized to certain hyperbolic quartic extensions, as well as certain families of Kummer extensions, enabling control of the rank in these contexts. Our work involves an in-depth analysis of the methods used to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within quadratic fields, as well as a discussion of the conditions necessary to extend these results to higher degree extensions. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This study highlights the potential of integrated quantum elements, combining multiple materials, to serve as quantitative proxies for research on material flaws causing decoherence. This terahertz near-field vision of quantum devices also enables the discovery of localized defects and material flaws at the microscale, facilitating device optimization and reducing loss channels. This research was conducted at the THz Near-Field Spectroscopy Unit at Aalto University, and the findings are relevant to quantum research and development taking place worldwide. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community and to guide future research and potential missions to study the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, as well as its complex interactions that have shaped and continue to shape Venus's evolution.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. One example, subthreshold neuronal activity, is presented as an application of these results. One interesting finding related to this example is that, contrary to expectations, there are instances where the Bayesian estimator incorrectly adds connections to the graph, even when the data duration is relatively long. One possible explanation for this phenomenon is offered by proving that its Bayesian estimator is asymptotically inconsistent, a novel finding that also extends the results of [13] beyond the linear case. One possible approach to evaluating the Bayesian estimator's performance is by conducting a simulation study on various configurations of the model. One such simulation involves altering one model parameter to see how this affects the graph's edge formation mechanism, which in turn affects the probability of correctly identifying that edge in the Bayesian estimator. One interesting observation from this simulation is that there are edges that are so weak that they cannot be discovered by the Bayesian estimator, even when the data set is extensive. One possible way to improve the performance of the Bayesian estimator on those weak edges is by increasing the number of data sets available to it, which in turn is possible by making one of the model parameters larger, which in turn makes the graph's edge formation mechanism more urgent, resulting in the Bayesian estimator detecting those weak edges, even when the data set is extensive. One possible alternative to the Bayesian estimator is a regularized $\ell_1$-based method, which is also known as the FOCUS method, that was previously introduced in [6]. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. If the input laser pulse contains a significant amount of elliptical polarization, the waveplate can maintain this inherent property while still increasing the peak power of the dominant linear polarization component. This suggests it can be used as a sophisticated component for finite amplitude laser pulse purification. This idea has been applied to demonstrate a method of nonlinear pulse compression based on polarization, which can be used to compress a circularly polarized laser pulse to approximately 2 times the duration of an initial pulse with the same peak power. This has been verified through simulations of different laser pulse combinations. This approach has been tested with simulations of both thin disk amplifiers and plasma-based amplifiers, which showed that this technique is effective in compressing laser pulses with a high level of bipolarity, resulting in a compression ratio of 2 for a specific pulse combination. This type of plasma waveplate offers a promising solution for the problem of laser pulse bipolarity in multi-petawatt laser systems, allowing for the conversion of excess linear polarization to additional peak power, which can be as simple as a magnetized plasma wave of a few centimeters in length. This has significant implications for the design and operation of future multi-petawatt laser systems, allowing for a level of self-correction and increasing the overall efficiency to near maximum capabilities. Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+ e^-$ collisions between the $\tau$-pair threshold and $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV is considered. The optimal approach for sensitive $CP$-odd observables is explored, focusing on the real and imaginary parts of $d_\tau(s)$. The expected outcomes for optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV with $\tau^\pm$ decaying into leptonic or semihadronic modes are calculated, accounting for full kinematic information. For the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator, with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$ and assuming acceptance cuts, the achievable sensitivities for $d_\tau$ are estimated to be $6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for semihadronic decays, respectively. In the ideal case without particle cuts, the achievable sensitivities with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, corresponding to $4.5 \times 10^{10}$ $\tau^+ \tau^-$ events, would be $5.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm, respectively. Additionally, the magnitude of the $\tau$ EDM form factor in the type-II two-Higgs doublet and scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model is investigated. The results show that the $\tau$ EDM form factor is generally the smallest among $\tau$, $K$, and barion EDMs in these two scenarios. The achievable sensitivities with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV also allow for the derivation of lower limits on the mass of these new physics scenarios: $m_{\text{IIHDDM}} \geq 93.6$ GeV, $m_{\text{SLQ}} \geq 652.6$ GeV, given the assumed values for the couplings and the relation between the EDM form factor and the mass of the particle and the energy of the collision. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In contrast, the existing rank metric decoding approach is only probabilistically effective, especially for code rates greater than half. In the course of our analysis, we establish a new ordering concept for vectors and utilize a concept previously proposed by the paper's first author. The new ordering is characterized as being compatible with the rank metric decoding architecture, and this fact is demonstrated through a relevant theorem. The paper also examines relationships between various orderings and provides a specific example of an ordered sequence of vectors. The novel decoding strategies are accompanied by specific examples and scenarios, which include the previously mentioned Gabidulin codes and the rank metric codes defined using the Vasil'ev construction. The paper's conclusions are completed by outlining potential avenues for further research. The proposed decoding methods can be implemented using a computer and are relatively straightforward, as they primarily involve basic matrix operations. The paper's results are applicable to codes defined using the rank metric and provide insights that can be more broadly applied. The paper is accompanied by an open problem, which is focused on finding an optimal decoding method for the rank metric errors. The paper also includes a bibliography of related references. Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams. This resulting expression can be compared to the original integral representation of the spinning block operator. The obtained geodesic Witten diagram representation can be seen as a two-parameter discretization of the original integral representation of the spinning block operator. The relationship between the AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagram representation and the original integral representation of the spinning block operator is explicitly captured by the "resolution" matrix, which can be deduced through a numerical analysis of the geodesic Witten diagrams or the integral representation of the spinning block operator. The resulting "resolution" matrix is found to be invariant under the exchange of the two spacetime coordinates, as well as under the change in spin value. The derived resolution matrix provides insight into the relationship between the AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagram and integral representation of the spinning block operator. The obtained results suggest that the spinning block operator representation can be understood as a continuous variation of a specific discrete geodesic Witten diagram. The obtained results also imply that the resolution matrix can be identified with the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients associated with the conformal group $so(2,1)$, which is realized through the fusion of two $so(2,1)$ representations. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we explore the connection between combinatorial Pontrjagin classes and their differentiable counterparts via a topological transformation, establishing that this relationship depends solely on the local topological properties of a neighborhood in a specific manifold. We then determine the precise coefficients for combinatorial Pontrjagin classes, demonstrating that they are equivalent to the differentiable ones after the transition is taken into account. Furthermore, we provide a straightforward, inductive proof for the accuracy of these coefficients. Lastly, we offer a final commentary on the underlying principles of combinatorial differentiable manifolds and the stability of combinatorial Pontrjagin classes.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. 

These models have been compared to established theories and the results obtained from them analyzed. Furthermore, we have used this method to investigate the effects of uncertainties in certain constants and the representation of the equation of state on the properties of rotating stars. 

This approach has been used to create detailed maps of stable and unstable configurations in rotating stars, and has also been applied to simulate the evolution of rotating stars during the process of cooling, demonstrating how their structures change over time. 

We have developed a publicly accessible code that solves the algebraic equations described above and have used this code to demonstrate our results, including the maps of unstable configurations and the detailed records of the evolution of rotating stars. 

These findings have significant implications for the interpretation of seismic data obtained from seismic waves generated by oscillations in rotating stars, and for the understanding of their evolutionary processes. 

We have also discovered that the process of cooling rotating stars leads to a state of instability at certain core radii, and have identified the factors that influence this state of instability, and the conditions under which it may lead to a collapse or a slowdown of the star's rotation. 

These discoveries have significant implications for the understanding of the evolution of rotating stars, and for the interpretation of seismic data obtained from seismic waves generated by oscillations in these stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that selective labeling coupled with active learning can achieve comparable results to traditional labeling methods, despite employing significantly less labeled data. Our proposed approach provides a significant advancement in the field of document extraction, by making the labeling process more efficient and expanding the scope of applicable documents to include those with visually rich layouts. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/selectedeo.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, comprising tools for data management, network training, and visualization. This platform recovers known neutron star and binary neutron star events with a purity of 0.45 and 0.25, respectively, and recovers 70% of binary black hole merger events with the correct mass ratio bin. We also demonstrate the robustness of this approach when applying it to future detectors. The development of this research is ongoing, and we highlight potential paths for its expansion. We conclude by examining the implications of these results for future detectors and provide theoretical background information on compact binary mergers and deep learning techniques. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era.
