Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. Finally, in models depicting dense stars or dense protostars, objects can get trapped in the inner region, leading to persistent accretion and potentially affecting the formation of massive stars through constraints like the core collapse type or mass. The possible timescales for completing accretion bursts and merging with stars also been determined, along with an analysis of actual bursts and mergers in young massive protostars, such as G333.65-0.15, IRAS 06301+1030, and W3(OH). The findings suggest that many high-mass stars undergo extensive mergers with stars or massive star clusters, while objects trapped in the inner region could result in stars with massive cores or massive H-rich envelopes, indicating that the relationship between high-mass star formation and gas and dust clouds may be more flexible than previously thought. The possible presence of trapped objects in the inner region also provides possible explanations for phenomena like massive H-rich stars, or the different collapse types, and offers a potential link to massive star formation being influenced by the formation of star clusters and massive star clusters formed from the merger of stars. The possible timescales for completing accretion bursts and merging with stars is approximately 0.4 million years, which is the timescale for completing the mass-gathering stage before transitioning to massive direct collapse or core collapse. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our research further explores the effects of vorticity on wave dynamics, revealing that it gives rise to oscillatory behavior in the wave envelope, and causing the envelope to shift due to the water's circular motion. Additionally, we analyze the statistics of wave amplitude, discovering that the distribution of the envelope's square is a Gamma distribution, which changes parameter values as the level of vorticity changes. Our findings also support the application of our model to related problems, such as wave interaction with surface tension and boundary walls. Our research underscores the significance of vorticity in shaping water dynamics and the intricate relationship between vorticity and water's surface elevation, emphasizing the complex, nonlinear relationships between these elements. We conclude by outlining potential future research avenues, including analyzing the effects of vorticity on wave behavior in limited domains, examining the role of vorticity in generating specific wave patterns, and investigating the link between vorticity and water's entropy. Our study of these issues has led to the development of a new, non-perturbative Hamiltonian Dysthe equation with constant vorticity, with values ranging from $\roise{10^{-3}}$ to $\roise{10^{3}}$, that accurately describes water wave dynamics in a wide range of scenarios. Our model enables the reliable simulation of water wave behavior across various levels of vorticity, even in situations characterized by intense water motion, and our analysis has uncovered the fundamental, Hamiltonian principles governing water wave dynamics in such environments. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, specifically the limitations of large pre-trained language models like BERT, as well as opportunities for further innovation in the field of fake news detection. The code is available at https://github.com/AhmedHamdy1991/CMTR-BERT.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. A specific case of L1-PCA without rotational invariance is introduced as a special case of the model's application. The development of a numerical implementation to solve the fundamental problem of robust clustering, the robust version of the K-means algorithm, is also presented. The code is publicly available on GitHub. The results obtained from the proposed algorithm on synthetic and real-world data were compared to two other state-of-the-art algorithms, both of which are based on a block-wise proximal alternating linearized minimization framework, and significant improvements in objective function values and clustering accuracy were observed. The proposed algorithm was found to be particularly effective in resolving clustered data, as demonstrated by a visualization of the cluster structure formed during the experiments. The development of an intuitive interpretation of the results presented by the proposed algorithm, particularly in the context of clustering, is also addressed in the study. The paper concludes by outlining potential future modifications to the algorithm, such as incorporating penalty terms and developing a version of the algorithm for online applications. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. To validate our findings, we employ a subset of the annotated EmoTalks dataset with 1,000 samples and discover that BERT's efficacy in annotation revision is comparable to that of human annotators. Furthermore, we discover that BERT's effectiveness in annotation revision increases in proportion to the complexity of the data set, as evidenced by our evaluation of two variant versions of the EMO20Q dataset. We are aware of only two possible approaches to evaluating annotated data containing complex semantic labels, and our research opens up new possibilities for exploiting NLP models to enhance the quality of such annotations. We make our code and annotated EMO20Q dataset available to the public. We also discuss two potential applications of BERT for validating and refining other annotated data sets containing complex semantic labels. In these cases, we simply use BERT to establish golden standards for evaluating the effectiveness of human annotators. Consequently, the quality of these datasets can be enhanced by recruiting fewer annotators. We propose a method to repurpose BERT as a validator of annotated data containing complex semantic labels, which entails training a classifier using BERT-based embeddings of paraphrased textual data. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This demonstrates the capabilities of atomic interferometry in detecting the Meissner effect and related properties, such as superconducting material parameters and local density fluctuations. Furthermore, this method could be scaled up to measure expelled fields in vacuum or in contact with matter, opening possibilities for research in quantum physics and chemistry. Although this concept was theoretically proposed for atomic Bose-Einstein condensates, it's also applicable to other matter waves, including those produced by optical lattices, and can be implemented using existing atomic interferometry setups. In its most basic form, detecting the Meissner effect through atomic interferometry involves precise control of magnetic fields, but in more complex configurations, it's possible to measure the expelling strength of superconductors, the spin-orbit coupling of 2D gases, or the electric field sensitivity of atomic levels. In these scenarios, the capability to measure the Meissner effect goes beyond local field detection and can be considered a novel form of matter-wave sensing. In addition to superconducting materials, this method can also be used to study the response of other quantum systems to external fields, providing valuable insights into their unique properties and behavior. Although implementing this concept on actual superconducting samples is challenging due to interferometer stability and scission issues, it's possible to overcome these difficulties by using advanced quantum technologies, such as nitric oxide-filled capillary interferometry, which combines the advantages of optical matter waves with the stability of magnetic samples. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework under an permissive BSD license to facilitate easy adoption across a range of object-oriented GPU applications.  Our framework source code is available at https://github.com/CompilersGroup/DynaSOAr.  We also include a brief DynaSOAr DSL language reference at the end of this document. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. This theoretical model highlights the complexity of YSR states caused by spin-orbit coupling, interaction with superconducting host materials, and the localized magnetic moments of the impurities. Furthermore, this framework facilitates prediction of unique phenomena for other magnetic dimers and layered structures, as well as other surfaces and materials. Given the limited scope of this study, suggestions are made for exploring other magnetic dimers, such as the Ni$_2$ dimer, and examining the interplay between Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states and host material bands. Given its limitations, this theoretical framework for the YSR states on Nb(110) awaits experimental verification through tunneling spectroscopy of magnetically coupled Ni dimer systems. This model's capabilities position it to explore novel phenomena associated with magnetic dimers and layered structures, as well as other surfaces and materials, by analyzing the interplay between the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, spin-orbit coupling, and the localized magnetic moments of the impurities. Given the restricted nature of this investigation, research directions are proposed, including examining the Ni$_2$ dimer, and investigating the interplay between the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states and host material bands. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, calculations highlight the significance of accurately describing electron-ion interactions, as well as the importance of distinguishing between different interaction ranges, which can influence the prediction of magnetic properties and bond lengths.  Suggested experiments include leveraging scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy to visualize and analyze the magnetic and electronic structures of such defects on the TiO2 surface.  Moreover, theoretical models can also be compared with these experimental findings to validate their accuracy.  Lastly, we propose that interstitial N defects could be responsible for N-O bonds found at surface and interface areas of TiO2 based devices, and that they may serve as sites for reactive oxygen species formation, enhancing the device's instability and influencing its performance.  Conversely, substituting some Ti atoms with carbon or nitrogen could result in nanocrystalline TiO2 materials, which may exhibit comparable or improved performance based applications such as solar energy, biomedicine, and catalysis.  Ultimately, this study demonstrates the versatility and toughness of TiO2, as well as the vast potential of TiO2 based materials in photocatalytic applications.  Conversely, we suspect that similar results may also be obtained for other d-block elements, which could be verified through the use of suitable supercells and codes to investigate the electronic and magnetic structures of d-block element doped

I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I discuss the potential discovery and characterization of the semi-elastic process using additional variables beyond rapidity of the forward proton. The required datasets and analysis patterns are outlined for achieving the aforementioned goals. The proposed elastic searches can be realized using a suitable trigger strategy that utilizes the LHC's forward proton detectors and zero-gap proton triggers which are currently available or soon will be, enabling the detection of rare top-quark decays and semi-elastic processes at the Large Hadron Collider. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we demonstrate that this lower bound approach can be applied to a broad category of substructures, thereby generating a numerous collection of new upper density values. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between graph factors and densities, introducing a compatible division where the Ramsey upper density of a given density $\delta$ is equivalent to the least $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$ and a maximum-possible edge density of $\delta$. We prove that this new density has the same value as its original counterpart, thereby confirming a conjecture initially proposed by the first author. Lastly, we establish a lower bound for the new density, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. To achieve over 90 percent accuracy, our estimates suggest that qutrits would require an order of magnitude more time (10^3 to 10^4 times) than qubits to simulate the same scenario. To facilitate the achievement of high-simulation accuracy in sQED, implementing error correction protocols or using noise-resilient operators could significantly improve the effectiveness of qudit simulations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlexanderCruzan/sQED-noise-analysis.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. The theoretical understanding of this phenomenon is supported by three separate simulation approaches, each validating the findings and providing a framework for predicting the degree of polarization in various scenarios. The positive outcomes of this research stem from the relatively easy implementation of targets with a high level of density, the inherent polarization of the laser fields, and the inevitable presence of intense magnetic fields within the positrons, emitted by interactive matter-month-long plasma. The potential uses of positively charged particles emitted at high intensities and significant polarization properties are considerable, with possible roles in advanced medical treatments, high-speed computing, and a wide range of astrophysical and cosmological studies. The findings of this research, along with its supporting simulations and theoretical analysis, pave the way for executing experiments that can replicate these effects and take advantage of their vast potential. The results of this study have been validated through the use of three separate simulation approaches, each with its own unique methodology, yet they all converge on the same outcome, emphasizing the robustness of the positively charged particle polarization and the ease with which it can be controlled and manipulated in experiments. The positive charge polarization emitted at high intensities is likely inseparable from its positive mass counterpart

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it demonstrates that groups with a polynomial diameter are soluble if their largest conjugacy class is minorated by a linear fraction. This research also presents examples and counterexamples to illustrate the proposed criteria for groups with a polynomial diameter. Specifically, it shows that there exist finite simple groups with a polynomial diameter, demonstrating that this group property is not soluble. This research also discovers that the largest possible diameter for the alternating group of degree 20 is exact, which can be compared to the existing bound for the symmetric group of degree 20. Additionally, it provides an upper bound for the diameter of the Coxeter group Scd(n), as well as a precise formula for the diameter of the dihedral group of order 2d. Lastly, it demonstrates that the diameter of a group that is close to being nilpotent of class two is directly proportional to its largest conjugacy class. This research also explores the relationship between the diameter of a group and the efficiency of its group action on a specific geometric space. Specifically, it demonstrates that a finite group G acts efficiently on a specific geometric space if and only if it contains a subset of elements with a diameter that scales exponentially in relation to the space's dimension. This research also provides an alternative proof of an existing result concerning the diameter of the symmetric group of degree 20. Lastly, it provides an alternative approach to defining the diameter of a group using the concept of distance in algebraic geometry. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. Furthermore, the temperature sensor's robustness was demonstrated in a real-world application, where it accurately monitored the temperature of a sub-threshold circuit while operating under dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The proposed temperature sensor has been patented as part of the project's activities (US 9,684,542 and SNIP 20160117-279). The design has also been made available to other researchers through an open-source framework. The research was funded by the EU FP7 project PRACTISE (GA no. 288535) and the Swedish Research Council (VR) project EASYSENSE (2013-4090). The authors would like to express their gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their valuable feedback, to the EU PRACTISE project for providing access to the 180nm process technology, and to STMicroelectronics for providing access to the 28nm process technology. The proposed temperature sensor has been successfully integrated into a 28nm FDSOI process, demonstrating excellent performance over a -40{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C temperature range, and has also been used to accurately monitor the temperature of a high-performance microprocessor core. The design of the temperature sensor has been patented

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks has been examined through the Atiyah sequence in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological groupoid extensions were defined along with their correspondence to gerbes over topological stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Moreover, the research delves into examining gerbes over Deligne Mumford stacks constructed through descent via the symplectic geometry approach developed by Bénabou and Gourel in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Additionally, it investigates connections between gerbes over stacks and Cech cocycles in the context of the classical definition employed by Gruault in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Furthermore, the study contributes an original finding that shows gerbes over Deligne Mumford stacks are equivalent to gerbes over the classification stack via the geometric structure of the groupoid in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Lastly, the research provides an unpublished result from [arXiv:2103.04560] that examines the relationship between line bundles over the classifying stack of a flat principal bundle. The main PhD contributions have been published in [arXiv:1907.00375, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2103.04560]. The underlying theory is explained through a series of lectures delivered at workshop titled "Geometry, Topology and Spin" held in St. Petersburg, Russia from the 21st to the 28th of July, 2014. The note also includes an unpublished result from [arXiv:1907.00375] that examines the relationship between line bundles over the classifying stack of a flat principal bundle. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Such an examination will be crucial in determining whether this correlation is an intrinsic feature of molecular cloud development or if it is a byproduct of external factors, specifically the relationship between star formation and gas displacement by infrared dark clouds.  Sensitive observations of chemical abundance within these cores may also provide additional insights into their evolutionary history.  Ultimately, resolving the detail of these processes will require the development of more sophisticated models that incorporate a wider range of observations and physical processes, particularly those related to the core formation and disintegration of molecular gas, and will necessitate the continued survey of extragalactic infrared dark clouds.  We have made preliminary assessments of the mass functions of both protostellar and starless cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud, and have compared these functions to that of the cloud's associated young stellar objects.  These comparisons have revealed an overlap between the mass ranges of both cores and the formed stars, with the exception of the most massive cores and stars.  These exceptions may be explained by the presence of massive protostars that have yet to reach their main sequence, and whose formation is a natural extension of the core formation process rather than a result of any discontinuity in the core or star formation processes.  We have also examined the distribution of core masses in relation to their surrounding environment, and have found that the mass function of the cores is uniformly distributed throughout the cloud, with no significant variation between different molecular outflows or associated young stellar objects.  These uniform distributions may be responsible for the lack of overlap between the mass functions of the cores and formed stars, with the exception of the most massive cores and stars. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The resulting operator leads to the desired one-dimensional recurrence. The process also involves recovering the modified expansion coefficients, thereby providing a complete solution for defining positive definite functions on the sphere through one-step recurrences. The paper also explores the relationship between these recurrences and the underlying geometric properties of the sphere, specifically involving the use of the monic and minimal Gegenbauer polynomials and a related convolution structure. The results presented in this paper have implications for the application of spectral methods in various contexts, including the solution of integral equations involving operators with smoothing properties. The one-dimensional recurrence can be employed to enforce the preservation of the positive definite property when the space dimension changes by one, which is a critical outcome for the accuracy of these methods. The paper concludes by discussing the computational efficiency of different methods available for transferring the positive definite property from one space dimension to another. The results presented in this paper have been applied to the specific example of the minimal Gegenbauer polynomials, which are essential in the solution of a significant problem in numerical analysis, specifically related to the characterization of the space in which a class of integral operators acts continuously. The paper also explores the relationship between the transfer of the positive definite property and the convergence of the associated recursion, which is a critical outcome for the accuracy of these methods. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The data and code used in this report are available at https://github.com/alexfawzi/iscnn.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. This improvement ensured reliable access to helicon mode across a wide range of magnetic fields, and allowed for flexible control of plasma density by adjusting the magnetic field, power, and electron temperature. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology enables researchers to demonstrate the significance of model performance for binary mask prediction alone, rather than on density mask prediction alone. Experimental evaluations conducted on three separate datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the W-Net model achieving superior performance compared to standard U-Net, LinkNet, and FPN models. Moreover, this approach has been applied to a limited amount of annotated density masks, which serves as a form of regularization, without limiting its general applicability. Finally, this model has been incorporated into a workflow that is capable of extracting valuable information from images with background, thus enhancing its practical utility. The open-source W-Net model, along with the code and datasets used in this research, are available for public use.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results indicate a 13 dB boost in the signal-to-noise ratio of lateral displacement estimates derived from VSSA in comparison to conventional SA, as well as a 50% reduction in the mean squared error of estimates obtained from VSSA in comparison to conventional SA. The outcomes of this research demonstrate the potential of VSSA in elastography applications, offering a platform for the development of novel elastography methods that integrate SA with OVERWIND. The technique's potential is further highlighted in a numerical elastography simulation, which shows that VSSA provides accurate estimates of mechanical properties in relation to ground truth values. The proposed approach is available online at https://github.com/ultrasonics-lab/VSSA-elastography. The findings of this research have implications for the improvement of elastography methods using SA, including the OVERWIND technique, and provide a framework for the assessment and analysis of these methods. The proposed technique can also be used as a platform for the development of novel elastography methods and ultrasound beamforming techniques. The potential of VSSA in combination with elastography techniques and ultrasound beamforming methods is yet to be fully explored and presents research opportunities for the scientific community. The technique's potential in combination with elastography techniques and ultrasound beamforming methods presents opportunities for the development of novel elastography methods, including elastography techniques based on SA, OVERWIND, and other methods, as well as ultrasound beamforming techniques based on VSSA.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that imperative algorithms are, in fact, a means of executing proofs, which provides insights that can be applied to specific problems. Additionally, this framework offers possibilities for generating imperative algorithms from the base of natural deduction, making it useful for developing educational content that teaches both computing and logical reasoning skills. In the process of developing this idea, we will delve into a step-by-step examination of how to derive a simple imperative algorithm from a related proof. The key components of this framework, including the relationship between natural deduction and imperative algorithms, are relevant to a broad range of topics including theoretical computing, logic, education, and software engineering. The presentation of this idea will be accessible to a wide range of audiences, spanning introductory college courses in computing and logic to advanced graduate-level topics in programming languages and the theory of logic-based programming. The underlying principles can be applied to various programming languages, making it compatible with multiple programming paradigms including but not limited to imperative, object-oriented, and functional computing. The translation of algorithms into equivalent proofs and the corresponding sequent calculus formulas can be expressed as a translation procedure, which is deterministic and reliable. The development of this framework for logical pseudocodes also includes a discussion of the related issues of input input values, the validation of the generated algorithms, and the possibility of forwarding reasoning. The compatibility of this approach with forward reasoning and the associated challenges are central to the discussion. The presentation concludes by examining three prominent examples, including a simple imperative algorithm, a more complex algorithm derived from natural deduction, and an algorithm generated through the translation of a computability logic web. The corresponding pseudocodes, algorithms, and the underlying logic are presented in a clear and easily understandable format. The compatibility of this approach with various programming languages and the associated challenges are also examined in the discussion of the three examples. The paper terminates by emphasizing the innovatory aspects of this research, which provides unprecedented insights

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We also achieve this achievement without sacrificing the accuracy of our results. Furthermore, our algorithm yields a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation of the optimal clustering cost within the radius of $\epsilon$ from $0$. In the event that the data stream finishes, our coreset algorithm provides a $O(kd\cdot \Delta)$-approximation of the optimal clustering cost. As for the update time, it takes $\Box$ time to update the coreset for a point addition or deletion. We have also explored a second pass algorithm to solve for the optimal clustering, taking $\Box \cdot k^2 \cdot d^2 \cdot \Delta^2$ time to compute the coreset, and subsequently $\Box \cdot k \cdot d^2 \cdot \Delta^2$ time to obtain the final clustering. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by focusing on macro-actions, our model can be adapted for application in large-scale real-world scenarios, including in robotics. All the code used in this research is publicly available. We further contribute a new hierarchical version of the 'Helicopter Game', in addition to the commonly used grid world examples, such as 'Cliff World' and 'Laser Tag'. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research highlights the challenges and opportunities in multi-task
reinforcement learning settings and showcases a straightforward yet effective way
to exploit task sharing, namely by employing modular models. Our code is available
at github.com/sfeng123/model-based-multi-task.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By combining these results, we derive several notable consequences and generalizations, including an undecidability result for certain formal systems and an unprovability statement for a specific arithmetic formula. This study's aim is to reveal the internal connections among these seminal theorems and demonstrate the cohesive nature of first-order arithmetic proofs. Moreover, we examine the initial reaction of logicians to these results and the development of the field since then. In doing so, this work offers an in-depth look at the groundbreaking research of its time and the profound impact it had on the advancement of mathematical logic. Despite the passage of time, these findings remain crucial to the field and continue to bear significant meaning for present-day philosophical debates surrounding Quine's New Foundations and the inherent properties of first-order arithmetic. Additionally, this work's results and conclusions are relevant to a broader logical context, encompassing both classical systems and their modern counterparts, such as Peano arithmetic and simpler formal systems. Lastly, this work is an extension of an earlier related study titled "Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem for the Formal System of Basic Logic" by the same author.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of sampled images. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shoukai2015/RCWGAN.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the surface area of this void is extremely small, about 2 x 10^18 cm^2, providing a unique insight into the morphology of the Local Bubble. The short rotation period of this orbit, equal to 79.998 days, was also utilized to calculate the screen's distance from the nearest solar system object, concluding that the screen's distance exceeds the orbital height of the Sun. Ultimately, this research highlights the capabilities of long-term pulsar scintillation observations and Earth orbitality as effective methods for uncovering the characteristics of the interstellar medium around the Solar system. The data from these observations have been made publicly available on the Pulsar Observatory of the Arecibo Ionization Experiment website. The findings related to PSR B1133+16 contribute significantly to the existing knowledge about the Local Bubble and the distribution of the interstellar medium within the Solar neighborhood. The analysis techniques utilized in this study can be applied to other pulsar scintillation observations, offering valuable insights into the properties of the interstellar medium along various lines of sight to the Galaxy. The associated code with this research, consisting of the scintillation screen modeling code and the Pulsar Observatory of the Arecibo Ionization Experiment website, is available for public use. The discovery of a rare screen associated with a localized void in the Local Bubble raises additional questions about the distribution of matter within this bubble and the formation mechanisms of such screens, both of which require further investigation. The insights gained from this research can be integrated with the findings from other observations of the Solar neighborhood, ultimately revealing the three-dimensional structure of the Local Bubble. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Human evaluator ratings reveal that the proposed method exceeds the baseline WN model in terms of quality and pitch accuracy for unseen frequency inputs. Moreover, QPNet delivers a perceptually indistinguishable quality from state-of-the-art text-to-speech models using a simple mel-embedded spectrum auxiliary feature. The code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Parandose/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this framework is utilized to recast and generalize results on the properties of shadows, specifically establishing connections to functors that detect cyclic structures and validating the shadows' preservation of cyclic properties through functors that ignore cyclic structures. Lastly, this theory is applied to investigate the properties of functors from the THH of a bicategory, leading to the identification of universal and particular shadows, and demonstrating that particular shadows are equivalent to functors that detect cyclic structures. This research was influenced by the findings of the author's previous paper, yet it has been expanded to accommodate more general contexts, allowing for applications beyond the realm of stable homotopy theory. Lastly, this framework is shown to directly relate to and generalize the properties of the trace functor, ending with some open discussion on possible further connections to the theory of Baazies and the universal circle functor.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zhoukui, along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset accessible at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/data/vggsound_source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and flexibility also enable it to be highly versatile, allowing it to be used in various settings, from classification to generation, by adjusting its formulation of graph operations. This paper provides an open-source implementation of LGCN, along with a Python toolbox for hyperbolic graph operations. It is anticipated that LGCN will serve as a foundation for future advancements in hyperbolic graph learning.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The generalization of our results to other geometries is discussed, with specific consideration given to the $fcc$ geometry typical of perovskite-like materials. The inclusion of phonon coupling is also briefly examined. The associated Python code is publicly available upon submission of this work. The possible analogies with other Hamiltonian contexts are discussed in the appendix. The results presented in this paper were used in a related paper titled: Multiorbital Coupling and Anomalous Magnetic Exchange in Rare-Earth Perovskites. The role of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing there is analyzed in depth. The related paper titled: Magnetic Anisotropy in Rare-Earth Perovskites: Role of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ Mixing, Cation Displacement, and Spin-Orbit Coupling also builds upon these findings. The results for the $fcc$ geometry typical of perovskite-like materials were used in a related paper titled: Direct Transformation of a Ferromagnetic Double Layer to Ferromagnetism in Bulk: The Case of La$_{1/4}$Sr$_{1/4}$Eu$_{1/2}$O$_3$. The related paper titled: Rare-Earth and Activator Ion Co-doping: A Route to Higher Temperature Multiorbital Kerbing Points also builds upon these findings. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also clarifies the relationship between absolute and relative quantum cohomology through the use of proper rational functions. The findings presented in this paper were initially established in scientific papers by Tang and Qiu, and by Tang, and are now presented in their current form. The main content of this paper consists of three sections. The first section provides an introduction to the related mathematical concepts and the findings of the research. The second section delves into the details of the results, while the third section explores potential future directions of the research. The paper also includes four appendices that contain additional mathematical proofs and calculations. The research on which this paper is based was conducted by the author in collaboration with Zulin Xie and Youhua Wang. The paper is organized in a way that each section and the four appendices can be understood on their own, without necessarily referencing the other sections or appendices. The main content of the paper is divided into three parts, with Part I consisting of sections 1-3, Part II consisting of sections 4-5, and Part III consisting of sections 6-7, with the four appendices that follow. The paper concludes with a bibliography of the referenced scientific papers. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our analysis and experiments demonstrated the capabilities of StyleGAN in medical imaging, paving the way for using GAN-based networks in healthcare. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application includes a user-friendly
graphical interface that simplifies data import, methodology selection, and
visualization customization. ViDaExpert is a Java-based application that
runs seamlessly on various operating systems. The tool offers pre-configured
scenarios for demonstration and educational purposes, as well as an
extensive library of 3D textures and objects that can be combined to create
custom 3D scenes. Furthermore, ViDaExpert enables easy data export to other
formats, including the STP (3D Structure Elucidation) format used in NMR spectroscopy. The application source code is available under the BSD license, and the application itself is available for free use. The development of ViDaExpert was funded by the NZ Government Fund and the University of Auckland. The application runs on Java 8 and above. The current version of ViDaExpert is 3.0.3. The application supports data sets in CSV, ARFF, and LOF files, as well as MS Excel files. The development of ViDaExpert was carried out by the Bioinformatics Group at the University of Auckland. The application was previously known as ViDaVis. The tool enables nonlinear visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial data.
